Umberto Eco cites Augustine as the most significant Christian thinker on the theological integration of ugliness into divine beauty.

Correction: Wittgenstein is mentioned, but no book title is given — yet Wittgenstein is not Plato. No citation for Plato exists. Re-evaluating: only Wittgenstein, Mann, Brecht, and Lull are referenced as authors without book titles. But Wittgenstein, Mann, and Brecht are mentioned as allusions, not as cited sources of ideas in the narrative sense. The only clear book citation is Ars Magna of Raymond Lull. The others are literary allusions, not citations of their works as sources of ideas. The rule says: 'Focus ONLY on citations that appear within the narrative prose.' The mention of Wittgenstein, Mann, and Brecht is in the context of Kroeber’s translation choices — not as authoritative sources of ideas, but as stylistic references. Therefore, only Raymond Lull’s Ars Magna qualifies as a cited book. The mention of Ecclesiastes is a book, but it is not attributed to an author — it is referred to by its title. The original author of Ecclesiastes is traditionally Solomon, but the text does not name him. The excerpt refers to 'the book of the Bible known as Ecclesiastes' without naming Solomon as author. Therefore, per rules, if no author is named, we cannot invent one. So only Raymond Lull is cited with a specific book title. The other references (Wittgenstein, Mann, Brecht) are person references without book titles. So we include them with title: null. But the rule says: 'If an author is mentioned as a source of ideas...' — are Wittgenstein, Mann, and Brecht mentioned as sources of ideas? The text says: 'he even inserted vague allusions to Mann and Brecht – this was not unfaithful to my original text, because I inserted allusions to Wittgenstein.' So Umberto Eco is saying that he inserted allusions to Wittgenstein, and Kroeber inserted allusions to Mann and Brecht. So Wittgenstein, Mann, and Brecht are cited as sources of allusions — i.e., as sources of ideas or stylistic references. Therefore, they qualify as person references. So we must include them with title: null.

book:web_3f6e9216.description: An essay by Umberto Eco originally published in The New York Review of Books in 1995, titled 'Ur-Fascism,' which outlines 14 characteristics of fascist ideology. The cited text 'How to Spot a Fascist' is a popular paraphrase or adaptation of this essay, often circulated online and sometimes misattributed as a standalone work. The translation mentioned (Richard Dixon and Alastair McEwen) refers to later English-language publications of Eco's collected essays.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Umberto Eco's work as the source of the essay, noting its translation history and publication context within Harvill Secker's series.

book:25188293.description: 'Translation is always a shift, not between two languages but between two cultures. A translator must take into account rules that are not strictly linguistic but, broadly speaking, cultural.' Umberto Eco is of the world's most brilliant and entertaining writers on literature and language. In this accessible and dazzling study, he turns his eye on the subject of translations and the problems the differences between cultures can cause. The book is full of little gems about mistranslations and misunderstandin...

book:8694005.description: The year is 1327. Franciscans in a wealthy Italian abbey are suspected of heresy, and Brother William of Baskerville arrives to investigate. When his delicate mission is suddenly overshadowed by seven bizarre deaths, Brother William turns detective. His tools are the logic of Aristotle, the theology of Aquinas, the empirical insights of Roger Bacon - all sharpened to a glistening edge by wry humor and a ferocious curiosity. He collects evidence, deciphers secret symbols and coded manuscripts, and digs into....
commentaries: Umberto Eco identifies his own novel as containing examples of occult ekphrasis, using detailed verbal descriptions of real historical artworks to reconstruct a period’s visual atmosphere.
Umberto Eco references his own novel to illustrate how fire, even when accidental, can serve as an instrument of erasure tied to ideological control.
Umberto Eco notes Eco’s shift from academic writing to fiction as a response to cultural changes, using the novel’s publication as a marker of his evolving public role.

book:59925.description: How do we know a cat is a cat? And why do we call it a cat? How much of our perception of things is based on cognitive ability, and how much on linguistic resources? Here, in six remarkable essays, Umberto Eco explores in depth questions of reality, perception, and experience. Basing his ideas on common sense, Eco shares a vast wealth of literary and historical knowledge, touching on issues that affect us every day. At once philosophical and amusing, Kant and the Platypus is a tour of the world of our sense...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this book as a reference for conceptual analysis related to translation and cultural adaptation.
Umberto Eco refers to his own prior work as a source for earlier engagement with the philosophical question of universal structures underlying language and translation.

book:10528.description:
..". not merely interesting and novel, but also exceedingly provocative and heuristically fertile." The Review of Metaphysics
..". essential reading for anyone interesting in... the new reader-centered forms of criticism." Library Journal
In this erudite and imaginative book, Umberto Eco sets forth a dialectic between open and closed texts.
"
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this book as one of his own foundational works on reader-response theory.
Umberto Eco references his own book as a prior analytical work used to contextualize a translation case study involving Alphonse Allais's story.

book:17856812.description:
Foucault's Pendulum (original title: Il pendolo di Foucault) is a novel by Italian writer and philosopher Umberto Eco. It was first published in 1988; the translation into English by William Weaver appeared a year later.
Foucault's Pendulum is divided into ten segments represented by the ten Sefiroth. The novel is full of esoteric references to the Kabbalah. The title of the book refers to an actual pendulum designed by the French physicist Leon Foucault to demonstrate the rotation of the earth, which has s...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references his own novel, Foucault’s Pendulum, as the object of Weaver’s translation work, using it to ground his discussion in a concrete, personal example of translation dilemmas.
Umberto Eco points to his own novel as a case of occult ekphrasis, where architectural description serves to preserve the lost visual reality of a physical space through literary means.
Umberto Eco references his own novel as a fictional exploration of the 'empty secret' phenomenon, illustrating how invented conspiracies can be mistaken for real ones by true believers.
Umberto Eco references Eco’s novel as a literary exploration of conspiracy theories and hermetic symbolism, likely as an example of fictionalized esotericism.

book:10513.description: From the early Dark Ages to the Renaissance it was widely believed that the language spoken in the Garden of Eden was a perfect language, expressing all possible things, and that all current languages were its decadent descendants. This is an investigation into the history of this idea.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this book as his own prior work that explores the historical concept of a perfect language, grounding his current argument in his earlier research.

book:23070.description:
"Eco's essays read like letters from a friend, trying to share something he loves with someone he likes.... Read this brilliant, enjoyable, and possibly revolutionary book." --George J. Leonard, San Francisco Review of Books
..". a wealth of insight and instruction." --J. O. Tate, National Review
"If anyone can make [semiotics] clear, it's Professor Eco.... Professor Eco's theme deserves respect; language should be used to communicate more easily without literary border guards." --The New York Times
"The li...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references this work as another key contribution to his theory of interpretation and semiotics.

book:13326582.description: Inventing the Enemycovers a wide range of topics on which Umberto Eco has written and lectured for the past ten years, from a disquisition on the theme that runs through his most recent novel, The Prague Cemetery--every country needs an enemy, and if it doesn't have one, must invent it--to a discussion of ideas that have inspired his earlier novels. Along the way, he takes us on an exploration of lost islands, mythical realms, and the medieval world. Eco also sheds light on the indignant reviews of James Jo...

book:10506.description:
After a violent storm in the South Pacific in the year 1643, Roberto della Griva finds himself shipwrecked-on a ship. Swept from the Amaryllis, he has managed to pull himself aboard the Daphne, anchored in the bay of a beautiful island. The ship is fully provisioned, he discovers, but the crew is missing.
As Roberto explores the different cabinets in the hold, he remembers chapters from his youth: Ferrante, his imaginary evil brother; the siege of Casale, that meaningless chess move in the Thirty Years' War...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites his own novel as a literary reconstruction of a historical anecdote, using it to illustrate the imagined mechanism of the dog and the weapon salve.

book:44326249.description: World-renowned physicist and bestselling author Stephen Hawking presents a revolutionary look at the momentous discoveries that changed our perception of the world with this first-ever compilation of seven classic works on physics and astronomy. His choice of landmark writings by some of the world's great thinkers traces the brilliant evolution of modern science and shows how each figure built upon the genius of his predecessors. On the Shoulders of Giantsincludes, in their entirety, On the Revolution of He...

commentaries: Umberto Eco cites his own earlier work to ground his evolving definition of signs in relation to deception and falsification.

book:25643984.description: Cos'e una tesi di laurea e a che cosa serve; la scelta dell'argomento; la ricerca del materiale; il piano di lavoro e la schedatura; la stesura; la redazione definitiva; conclusioni.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Eco's book as the source of pedagogical tone and standards, highlighting its empathetic and rigorous approach to thesis writing.
Umberto Eco cites Eco's practical advice on organizing research materials as enduring and methodologically significant, even amid technological change.
Umberto Eco highlights Eco’s view that the value of a thesis lies in the disciplined process of research rather than the final topic, framing it as a formative educational experience.
Umberto Eco interprets Eco’s filing system as a philosophical practice—an ordering of the mind that values procedure over outcome and cultivates accuracy and intellectual pleasure.
Umberto Eco notes Eco’s broader literary and intellectual approach, using his thesis guide as an extension of his lifelong commitment to making humanities discourse engaging and accessible.
Umberto Eco references Eco’s recognition of systemic educational challenges, portraying the book as a response to democratized higher education without compromising rigor.
Umberto Eco cites Eco’s own words to underscore his awareness of the social expansion of higher education and his commitment to inclusive academic standards.
Umberto Eco presents Eco’s concept of academic humility as a core ethical principle in scholarly work, balancing openness with critical judgment.
Umberto Eco cites Eco's work on translation as a reference point, though the citation appears in a translator's footnote rather than within the main narrative.

book:93630.description: The well-known Italian semiotician and novelist Umberto Eco discloses for the first time to English-speaking readers the unsuspected richness, breadth, complexity, and originality of the aesthetic theories advanced by the influential medieval thinker Thomas Aquinas, heretofore known principally as a scholastic theologian. Inheriting his basic ideas and conceptions of art and beauty from the classical world, Aquinas transformed or modified these ideas in the light of Christian theology and of developments in...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Eco's work to illustrate a scholarly correction of Maritain's misattribution of Aquinas's definition of beauty, using it as a key reference for accurate Thomistic interpretation.

book:54270.description: Madman, tyrant, animal - history has given Adolf Hitler many names. In Mein Kampf (My Struggle), often called the Nazi bible, Hitler describes his life, frustrations, ideals, and dreams. Born to an impoverished couple in a small town in Austria, the young Adolf grew up with the fervent desire to become a painter. The death of his parents and outright rejection from art schools in Vienna forced him into underpaid work as a labourer. During the First World War, Hitler served in the infantry and was decorated....
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Mein Kampf as the definitive ideological text of Nazism, contrasting its systematic philosophy with the ideological incoherence of Italian Fascism.
Umberto Eco cites Hitler’s Mein Kampf as a later, racially charged extension of antisemitic tropes, linking Jewish appearance to moral and social corruption.

book:12075.description: Perhaps the most important work of philosophy written in the twentieth century, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicuswas the only philosophical work that Ludwig Wittgenstein published during his lifetime. Written in short, carefully numbered paragraphs of extreme brilliance, it captured the imagination of a generation of philosophers. For Wittgenstein, logic was something we use to conquer a reality which is in itself both elusive and unobtainable. He famously summarized the book in the following words: 'What can....
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Wittgenstein's Tractatus as a landmark work in contemporary philosophy, using it as a reference point to illustrate the importance of clarity in academic writing.

book:147476.description: Winston Smith is a low-rung member of the Party, the ruling government of Oceania. He works in the Ministry of Truth, the Party's propoganda arm, where he is in charge of revising history. He is but a small brick in the pyramid that is the Party, at the head of which stands Big Brother. Big Brother the infallible. Big Brother the all-powerful. In a totalitarian society, where individuality is suppressed and freedom of thought has its antithesis in the Thought Police, Winston finds respite in the company of....
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four as a referenced text, acknowledging its copyright and permission for excerpt use.

Umberto Eco cites Orwell’s novel as a literary embodiment of the institutionalized cultivation of the enemy, using Goldstein as a symbolic figure to sustain societal control through manufactured hatred.

book:42425.description:
From the cover of the first edition:
Into this great new novel--nearly twice as long as "A Farewell to Arms"--Ernest Hemingway has poured the fullness of his experience, the perfection of his art. A novel of wartime Spain, in which a young American and a Spanish girl live a lifetime of love and courage in four momentous days, it speaks with final and unforgettable power for the truth--the truth of war and life in our time.
With Robert Jordan already behind the enemy lines on his dangerous mission--to join f...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Hemingway’s novel as evidence that the term 'Fascist' was used broadly during the Spanish Civil War to describe enemy forces, even when they were technically Falangists.

book:13270.description:
'The plot is the source and the soul of tragedy'
In his near-contemporary account of Greek tragedy, Aristotle examines the dramatic elements of plot, character, language and spectacle that combine to produce pity and fear in the audience, and asks why we derive pleasure from this apparently painful process. Taking examples from the plays of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, The Poetics introduces into literary criticism such central concepts as mimesis('imitation'), hamartia('error'), and katharsis('purif...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Aristotle's Poetics as the foundational text that Averroes struggled to interpret due to cultural differences, highlighting the challenges of cross-cultural translation of literary concepts.
Umberto Eco cites Aristotle's Poetics as the authoritative source for the concept of anagnorisis, using it to ground the analysis of narrative structure in serialized novels.
Umberto Eco cites Aristotle's Poetics as a foundational text whose ideas influenced Renaissance thought, suggesting its relevance for scholarly interpretation.

book:551356.description: Aristotle, great Greek philosopher, researcher, reasoner, and writer, born at Stagirus in 384 BCE, was the son of Nicomachus, a physician, and Phaestis. He studied under Plato at Athens and taught there (367 47); subsequently he spent three years at the court of a former pupil, Hermeias, in Asia Minor and at this time married Pythias, one of Hermeias s relations. After some time at Mitylene, in 343 2 he was appointed by King Philip of Macedon to be tutor of his teen-aged son Alexander. After Philip s death....
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Aristotle’s De caelo as a key philosophical work on cosmology that influenced medieval astronomical thought.

book:208036.description: Metaphysics (Greek: ta meta ta phusika) is one of the principal works of Aristotle & the first major work of the branch of philosophy with the same name. The principal subject is "being qua being", or being understood as being. It examines what can be asserted about anything that exists just because of its existence & not because of any special qualities it has. Also covered are different kinds of causation, form & matter, the existence of mathematical objects, & a prime-mover God.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Aristotle’s Metaphysics as a foundational source for defining identity in the context of counterfeiting, using it to ground a practical criterion for sameness over abstract philosophical notions.
Umberto Eco cites Aristotle's Metaphysics as a key source for philosophical inquiry into being and first principles.
Umberto Eco cites Aristotle’s foundational text, implying it is referenced for its philosophical treatment of being, truth, or essence.

book:13457671.description:
One of the seminal works of Western philosophy, Aristotle's Rhetoric vastly influenced all subsequent thought on the subject -- philosophical, political, and literary. Focusing on the use of language as both a vehicle and a tool to shape persuasive argument, Aristotle delineates with remarkable insight both practical and aesthetic elements and their proper combination in an effective presentation, oral or written. He also emphasizes the role of language in achieving precision and clarity of thought.
The anc...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Aristotle's Rhetoric alongside the Poetics as a key Aristotelian work that shaped Renaissance scholarly engagement with classical texts.

book:550463.description:
Pliny the Elder, tireless researcher and writer, is author of the encyclopedic "Natural History," in 37 books, an unrivaled compendium of Roman knowledge.
The contents of the books are as follows. Book 1: table of contents of the others and of authorities; 2: mathematical and metrological survey of the universe; 3-6: geography and ethnography of the known world; 7: anthropology and the physiology of man; 8-11: zoology; 12-19: botany, agriculture, and horticulture; 20-27: plant products as used in medicine;....
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Pliny’s encyclopedic work as a source for ancient conceptions of monsters and natural wonders.

book:60408.description: When it first appeared in 1975, After Babel created a sensation, quickly establishing itself as both a controversial and seminal study of literary theory. In the original edition, Steiner provided readers with the first systematic investigation since the eighteenth century of the phenomenology and processes of translation both inside and between languages. Taking issue with the principal emphasis of modern linguistics, he finds the root of the "Babel problem" in our deep instinct for privacy and territory,....
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this book as a foundational theoretical work on translation, referenced directly by title and publication details.
Umberto Eco references Steiner's work as a key theoretical source on translation, likely drawing on its analysis of linguistic and cultural negotiation.

Umberto Eco cites Steiner's book 'After Babel' as a foundational text in translation theory, referencing it multiple times in the context of broader discussions on linguistic and cultural negotiation in translation.
Umberto Eco cites Steiner's 'After Babel' as a benchmark for translation theory due to its rich use of quotations, contrasting it with insufficiently exemplified works.
Umberto Eco cites Steiner’s After Babel to argue that translation involves navigating cultural and encyclopedic gaps, not just linguistic ones.

book:849877.description: As Joris-Karl Huysmans predicted in 1884, Against Nature (A rebours) was fated to be a novel like no other. Resisting the models of classic nineteenth-century fiction, it focuses on the attempts of its anti-hero, the hypersensitive neurotic and aesthete Des Esseintes, to escape Paris and the vulgarity of modern life. Holed up in his private museum of high taste, he indulges his pleasure in fine art and literature. A compendium of fin-de-siecle cultural decadence, Against Nature anticipates strains of modern...
commentaries: Umberto Eco invokes Huysmans’s novel À rebours as a literary parallel to Camporesi’s method of scholarly excavation, drawing a comparison between the protagonist’s rediscovery of medieval texts and Camporesi’s analysis of historical bodily narratives.

book:web_01e2766c.description: A foundational work in phonology and linguistic analysis by Roman Jakobson, originally published as part of the MIT Press series on speech and language studies. It presents a structuralist approach to speech sounds and their functional roles in language.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Jakobson’s work as one of three foundational contemporary texts for understanding structuralist theories of metaphor.

book:web_da5c12f5.description: The Carta Capuana is a legal document written in the vernacular of southern Italy in 960, widely regarded as the earliest known text in a Romance language that can be classified as early Italian. It is a notarial deed from the Abbey of Capua, documenting a land transaction.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references the Carta Capuana as a culturally significant historical text, used to evoke Italian literary heritage for his readers.

book:web_1e0afdad.description: A medieval Latin liturgical drama, also known as the 'Feast of Cyprian', composed around 965 CE. It is a dramatic representation of the Last Supper and the Passion of Christ, written in a mixture of prose and verse, and is one of the earliest examples of liturgical drama in Western Europe.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this medieval text as a primary literary model for the dream sequence in The Name of the Rose.

book:web_03c08f1d.description: Two medieval Germanic incantations or charms written in Old High German, discovered in a manuscript from the 9th or 10th century. They are the oldest known texts in the German language and contain pagan magical formulas, preserved in a manuscript from the Merseburg Cathedral.
commentaries: Umberto Eco acknowledges this text as the oldest German document, used by translator Kroeber to substitute the Carta Capuana for a German-speaking context.

book:web_b7475740.description: A 13th-century Spanish pilgrimage narrative, written in verse, describing the journey of a pilgrim to the Holy Land. It is one of the earliest known examples of Spanish prose fiction and is often compared to other medieval Spanish texts like El Cantar de Mío Cid for its linguistic and stylistic features.
commentaries: Umberto Eco mentions Fazienda de Ultramar as an old text with borrowed vocabulary, used by the translator as a model for inventing an archaic Spanish equivalent.

book:web_ccfee329.description: A medieval ecclesiastical text, likely composed in the 9th or 10th century, included in the Decretum of Burchard of Worms (c. 1020). It denounces the belief in witchcraft and nocturnal flights as delusions inspired by Satan, reflecting the Church's stance against pagan superstitions. The text is not authored by a single individual but is a canonical decree attributed to an anonymous bishop.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites the Canon episcopi as an early medieval ecclesiastical text that dismissed witch beliefs as delusions, contrasting it with later inquisitorial views that treated witches as real threats.

book:14487222.description: The Turba Philosophorum or assembly of the alchemical philosophers, is one of the earliest Latin alchemical texts, probably dating from the 12th century. It introduced many of the key themes of the alchemical tradition and was often quoted in later writings.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites the Turba philosophorum to support the idea that alchemical texts, though cryptic, are internally consistent and reveal their secrets to persistent inquiry.
Umberto Eco cites this medieval alchemical text to illustrate the consensus among alchemists that their symbolic language, though cryptic, consistently points to a single hidden truth.

book:web_f627fedb.description: An early Christian text of unknown authorship, written between the 2nd and 5th century CE, that describes animals, real and mythical, with moral and allegorical interpretations. It was highly influential in medieval bestiaries and Christian iconography.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites the Physiologus as a foundational medieval bestiary text that transmitted legendary and symbolic descriptions of animals and monsters, shaping medieval aesthetic views of the grotesque.

book:web_972558d5.description: An influential 1813 essay by German theologian and philosopher Friedrich Schleiermacher, in which he distinguishes between translation approaches that either move the reader toward the author (foreignizing) or the author toward the reader (domesticating). It is a foundational text in translation studies.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Schleiermacher’s work to present the dual view that language constrains thought, yet also allows for human agency in shaping linguistic boundaries.

book:web_a6917ec1.description: A one-sentence microfiction by Augusto Monterroso, first published in 1959 as part of his collection 'El dinosaurio'. It is widely regarded as the shortest novel ever written in Spanish and a landmark of minimalist literature.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Monterroso's micro-novel as an example to contrast intersemiotic adaptation with verbal translation, using it to illustrate the limits of fidelity in non-verbal media.

book:631010.description: " Il y a dans Les Mysteres de Paris une energie sauvage : celle d'une cohorte de personnages malefiques, malfrats hideux comme la Chouette, Tortillard - un anti-Gavroche -, le Maitre d'ecole ou Bras-Rouge, criminels du grand monde comme le comte de Saint-Remy, monstres hypocrites comme le notaire Jacques Ferrand. Eugene Sue n'est pas avare de noirceur. Mais il y a aussi une sauvagerie du Bien, celle de Rodolphe, prince melancolique venu a Paris a la recherche de sa fille perdue, impitoyable avec les mechant...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Sue's novel as an example of a literary work that has undergone translation, likely invoked to illustrate issues of cultural adaptation in translation.
Umberto Eco references Sue’s novel as the direct inspiration for Dumas’s The Count of Monte-Cristo, noting its cultural impact and subsequent decline in readability.

Umberto Eco cites Eugène Sue’s novel as an example of Romantic-era grotesque characterization, using its vivid description of the Schoolmaster to support the theme of excess in depictions of ugliness.
Umberto Eco uses this novel as a prime example of how narrative tradition and commercial serialization force premature revelations, undermining suspense despite clear reader anticipation.
Umberto Eco cites this description to show how literary portrayals of beauty can diverge from modern visual interpretations and require contextual analysis.

book:web_39b0f7be.description: A serialized novel by French author Eugène Sue, first published in 1845–1846, which tells the story of a cursed immortal Jew who wanders the earth as punishment for his role in the crucifixion of Jesus. It was part of Sue's popular series of social and political novels that critiqued contemporary society.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Sue’s novels as influential popularizers of the Jesuit conspiracy theory, showing how fiction amplified and disseminated the myth in the 19th century.
Umberto Eco cites this novel as a cultural reference point, possibly for its symbolic representation of eternal exile or guilt.

book:web_23b33605.description: A serialized novel by French author Eugène Sue, published in 1849–1856, which critiques social inequality and explores the lives of the working class through a dramatic, episodic narrative. It was one of the most popular and influential serialized novels of the 19th century.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Sue’s other serialized novel alongside The Wandering Jew as a major vehicle for spreading Jesuit conspiracy narratives to a broad public audience.

book:899896.description: The stories of twenty of Shakespeare's most popular plays
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites 'Tales from Shakespeare' by Charles and Mary Lamb as a preposterous example of paraphrase, using it to illustrate how interpretation can distort the original form.

book:999513.description: This gaudy, wild, and raw tale of a war-torn 17th Century Europe depicts Simplicissimus as the eternal innocent, the simple-minded survivor. We follow him from an orphaned childhood to the casual atrocities of occupying troops, through his own soldiering adventures, and up to his final vocation as a hermit alone on an island. Mike Mitchell's superb translation allows readers to enjoy more fully one of the great masterpieces of European literature and the first German bestseller.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Simplizissimus as another instance of a picaresque narrative that, like fairy tales, transmits archetypal structures across cultural forms.

book:22158284.description: In this new 2014 edition of The Waste Land, the text of Eliot's 1922 masterpiece is accompanied by Eliot's own knotty notes. For ease of reading, this Mask Press Edition presents The Waste Land as it first appeared in the American edition (Boni & Liveright), with Eliot's notes at the end. Eliot's own notes provides readers with invaluable materials on The Waste Land's sources, composition, and publication history.
commentaries: Umberto Eco uses Eliot’s The Waste Land as a counterexample to double coding, noting its reliance on explicit footnotes rather than implicit, layered irony.

book:2363017.description: Growing up is never easy; especially if your name happens to be David Copperfield. Orphaned as an infant, David must suffer the privation and cruelties of his evil stepfather, Mr.Murdstone; who packs David away to a workhouse at the age of ten! a trusting but vulnerable boy and practically alone in the world, David finds himself time after time at the mercy of a rogue's gallery of characters; the dashing but deceitful Steerforth, the detestable clerk Uriah Heep, and, last but not least, the beautiful but di...
commentaries: Umberto Eco uses Dickens's 'David Copperfield' as a paradigmatic example of how translation must convey not only narrative but also historical and stylistic context.
Umberto Eco cites Dickens's Hard Times as the seminal literary depiction of industrial ugliness, marking the beginning of a tradition in modern literature.

book:7480592.description: Gils Blas recounts the education and swashbuckling adventures of an adaptable young valet as he progresses from one master to the next, making his way from naive youth to cunning servant to landed proprietor and nobleman--with a stint in jail, bereavements, and fits of remorse along the way. Finally, our hero learns compassion and achieves tranquillity in a life in the country.
commentaries: Umberto Eco includes Gil Blas as an example of a literary work that embodies the same archetypal simplicity as fairy tales and myths, placing it in a lineage of popular narrative forms.

book:957691.description:
Le narrateur rencontre, dans un autobus, un jeune homme au long cou, coiffe d'un chapeau orne d'une tresse au lieu de ruban. Le jeune homme echange quelques mots assez vifs avec un autre voyageur, puis va s'asseoir a une place devenue libre. Un peu plus tard, le narrateur rencontre le meme jeune homme en grande conversation avec un ami qui lui conseille de faire remonter le bouton superieur de son pardessus.
Cette breve histoire est racontee quatre-vingt-dix-neuf fois, de quatre-vingt-dix-neuf manieres diff...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Queneau's 'Exercices de style' as a work he personally translated, highlighting the depth of reflection involved in the process.
Umberto Eco cites Queneau's Exercices de style as a model for translational creativity, where the translator replicates linguistic games rather than literal meaning.

book:3646333.description:
Alexandre Dumas
Alexandre Dumas lahir di Villers-Cotterets, Perancis, tanggal 24 Juli 1802. Kakeknya soerang bangsawan, neneknya wanita berkulit hitam dari Santo Domingo. Ayahnya seorang jenderal balatentara Napoleon, yang gugur pada saat Dumas baru berumur empat tahun, tanpa meninggalkan kekayaan sedikit pun. Ia dipelihara oleh seorang pendeta, kemudian bekerja sebagai juru tulis kantor pengacara. Pada saat usia dua puluh satu tahun ia pindah ke Paris, mengabdi pada seorang bangsawan. Perkenalannya dengan....
commentaries: Umberto Eco repeatedly cites Monte-Cristo as a case study in how a linguistically flawed novel can achieve literary status through narrative archetypes and structural wisdom.
Umberto Eco reiterates Monte-Cristo as an exemplar of a 'sludgy simple form'—a long novel that achieves mythic power despite stylistic shortcomings.
Umberto Eco analyzes Monte-Cristo as a narrative deeply structured by Christological archetypes, elevating it beyond its stylistic flaws through mythic resonance.
Umberto Eco cites Dumas’s memoir to highlight the enduring reality of fictional characters compared to historical figures, emphasizing the power of literary creation.
Umberto Eco cites Dumas’s The Count of Monte Cristo as an example of how excess and stylistic flaws, when amplified, can produce a Kantian sublime effect in literature.

book:742106.description:
One of the most celebrated & popular historical romances ever written. The Three Musketeers tell the story of the early adventures of the young Gascon gentleman d'Artagnan & his three friends from the regiment of the King's Musketeers-Athos, Porthos & Aramis.
Under the watchful eye of their patron M. de Treville, the four defend the honour of the regiment against the guards of the Cardinal Richelieu, & the honor of the queen against the machinations of the Cardinal himself as the power struggles of 17th-cen...
commentaries: Umberto Eco contrasts The Three Musketeers with Monte-Cristo, praising it as a well-crafted example of narrative energy, despite Dumas’s commercial motivations.
Umberto Eco references The Three Musketeers as a contrasting example of Dumas’s superior craftsmanship, used to highlight the deliberate excess in The Count of Monte Cristo.
Umberto Eco cites Dumas’s The Three Musketeers as the authoritative textual source for the character D’Artagnan, contrasting popular perception with the original narrative detail.

book:848993.description: Lombardo and Bell have translated this important early dialogue on virtue, wisdom, and the nature of Sophistic teaching into an idiom remarkable for its liveliness and subtlety. Michael Frede has provided a substantial introduction that illuminates the dialogue's perennial interest, its Athenian political background, and the particular difficulties and ironic nuances of its argument.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Plato’s Protagoras to introduce a mythological framework for understanding the origin of human faculties, drawing a parallel between divine creation and artistic alchemy.

book:17794748.description:
The dialogue takes place the day after Socrates described his ideal state. In Plato's works such a discussion occurs in the Republic. Socrates feels that his description of the ideal state wasn't sufficient for the purposes of entertainment and that "I would be glad to hear some account of it engaging in transactions with other states" (19b).
Hermocrates wishes to oblige Socrates and mentions that Critias knows just the account (20b) to do so. Critias proceeds to tell the story of Solon's journey to Egypt w...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Plato’s Timaeus to illustrate the philosophical foundation of geometric harmony as a criterion of beauty.

book:31846068.description:
Valtio on Platonin kuuluisin dialogi ja kiistaton paateos. Se on yhteiskuntateoria ja poliittinen utopia, jonka pohjaksi Platon joutuu esittamaan etiikkansa, ihmiskasityskensa, kasvatusoppinsa, politiikkansa, taideteoriansa ja metafysiikkansa.
Valtioon sisaltyy "koko Platon", ja siita lahtevat aatehistorialliset juonteet yltavat meidan paiviimme. Platon on alustavasti perustellut niin totuuden etsimisen kuin sensuurin, propagandan, syntyvyyden saannostelyn, vapaan kasvatuksen, feminismin, yhteisomistuksen j...
commentaries: Umberto Eco permits citing Plato's Republic in translation when the thesis topic is outside classical studies, emphasizing the necessity of specifying the translation edition used.

book:167803.description: L'expression roman fleuvedevrait, sans connotation pejorative, designer une oeuvre qui prend le temps de charrier mille petites particules d'impression pour les infuser dans l'esprit d'un lecteur captive. En somme, elle devrait avoir ete creee pour designer La Rechercheproustienne, qui s'ouvre Du cote de chez Swannet s'acheve une fois Le Temps retrouve. Dans le premier tome de ce superbe travail sur la memoire et la metaphore, oeuvre a part entiere mais aussi amorce dramatique d'un joyau de la langue franca...
commentaries: Umberto Eco uses Proust's 'À la recherche' as a canonical text to exemplify how interpretive inference differs from translation, highlighting the Oulipo's playful re-reading of its opening line.
Umberto Eco uses Proust’s text to highlight the discrepancy between an author’s stated aesthetic preferences and the artistic ideals their writing may imply.

book:124095.description: A stunning volume of philosophical reflections, short narratives, and prose poems, Pleasures and Daysprovides an early glimpse into Proust's genius as a collector of exquisitely poignant sensations and recollections. Set amid the salon society of fin-du-siecle Paris, these sketches and short stories depict the lives, loves, manners, and motivations of a host of characters, all viewed with a famously knowing eye. By turns cuttingly satirical and bitterly moving, Proust's portrayals are layered with imagery a...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Proust's work as a philosophical justification for valuing bad music due to its deep social and emotional resonance.
Umberto Eco quotes Proust’s reflection on the imperfect tense in Pleasures and Days to illustrate how linguistic form can evoke existential melancholy and artistic insight.

book:248193.description:
Lost in an art--the art of translation. Thus, in an elegant anagram (translation = lost in an art), Pulitzer Prize-winning author and pioneering cognitive scientist Douglas Hofstadter hints at what led him to pen a deep personal homage to the witty sixteenth-century French poet Clement Marot."
Le ton beau de Marot" literally means "The sweet tone of Marot", but to a French ear it suggests "Le tombeau de Marot"--that is, "The tomb of Marot". That double entendre foreshadows the linguistic exuberance of this....
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Hofstadter's book as a key reference for understanding the aesthetic challenges of translating poetic form, particularly the tercet structure of Dante's Divine Comedy.

book:web_75de9972.description: A famous modernist poem by Paul Valéry, first published in 1920, reflecting on mortality, time, and the sea. It is one of the most celebrated works of 20th-century French poetry.
commentaries: Valéry’s poem is referenced as a literary example in discussions of poetic translation, likely to demonstrate challenges in preserving form and meaning across languages.

book:1858271.description: "Nun ist gewiss praktische Philosophie nicht selber solche Vernunftigkeit. Sie ist Philosophie, das heisst, sie ist eine Reflexion, und zwar uber alles, was menschliche Lebensgestaltung zu sein hat. Im selben Sinne ist die philosophische Hermeneutik nicht selbst die Kunst des Verstehens, sondern die Theorie derselben. Aber die eine wie die andere Form von Bewusstmachung steigt aus der Praxis auf und bleibt ohne sie ein blosser Leerlauf. Das ist der besondere Sinn von Wissen und Wissenschaft, den es von der....
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Gadamer's work as a foundational text in her discussion of translation and the translator's horizon, implying its relevance to her theoretical framework.

book:web_c10cc4be.description: A lyric poem by Italian Romantic poet Giacomo Leopardi, widely regarded as one of the greatest works of Italian literature, meditating on infinity, solitude, and the human condition.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Leopardi's poem 'L’infinito' as a canonical literary reference in Italian Romanticism, essential for understanding the intertextual layer in his novel where the hedge evokes a shared cultural memory.
Umberto Eco references Leopardi’s poem as a philosophical meditation on infinity and human limitation, likely invoked in discussions of existential or aesthetic themes.

book:web_0d9ed66e.description: A collection of poems by Italian poet Giacomo Leopardi, first published in 1835. 'Les chants' is the French translation of 'Canti', translated by Michel Orcel and published in 1982 by L’Age d’Homme.
commentaries: Umberto Eco mentions this translated edition to illustrate the complexity of translation, particularly how translator choices (e.g., using 'sorcio' for 'rat') reflect linguistic and cultural negotiation, though the original work itself is not analyzed.

book:18490595.description:
A groundbreaking translation of the epic work of one of the great minds of the nineteenth century.
Giacomo Leopardi was the greatest Italian poet of the nineteenth century and was recognized by readers from Nietzsche to Beckett as one of the towering literary figures in Italian history. To many, he is the finest Italian poet after Dante. (Jonathan Galassi's translation of Leopardi's Canti was published by FSG in 2010.)
He was also a prodigious scholar of classical literature and philosophy, and a voracious....
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Leopardi’s Zibaldone to anchor the philosophical notion of perfection as essential completeness, linking medieval theology to Romantic-era thought.
Umberto Eco references Leopardi’s notebook as a repository of profound philosophical and literary reflections, likely for its depth of thought.

book:1010394.description: This essential introduction to the poems of Giacomo Leopardi provides a complete translation of The Canti, explanatory notes, and a selection of Leopardi's prose keyed to related poems. Further background is provided by an introduction and a brief biography woven from Leopardi's own words.
commentaries: Umberto Eco quotes Leopardi’s poem as an example of lyrical expression, citing its inclusion in a collected edition.

book:16248656.description: Willard Van Orman Quine begins this influential work by declaring, "Language is a social art. In acquiring it we have to depend entirely on intersubjectively available cues as to what to say and when." As Patricia Smith Churchland notes in her foreword to this new edition, with "Word and Object" Quine challenged the tradition of conceptual analysis as a way of advancing knowledge. The book signaled twentieth-century philosophy's turn away from metaphysics and what Churchland calls the "phony precision" of c...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this work as a reference point, likely for its theoretical framework on language and meaning, though no specific idea from the book is elaborated in the excerpt.
Umberto Eco cites Quine’s book as a referenced source in the footnote, indicating its relevance to the theoretical underpinnings of translation discourse.

book:17818767.description: Aeschylus was the first of the three ancient Greek tragedians whose plays can still be read or performed, the others being Sophocles and Euripides. He is often described as the father of tragedy: our knowledge of the genre begins with his work and our understanding of earlier tragedies is largely based on inferences from his surviving plays. Only seven of his estimated seventy to ninety plays have survived into modern times. Fragments of some other plays have survived in quotes and more continue to be disco...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Aeschylus’s Agamemnon as a prime example of ancient textual density, using it to illustrate how translation must reconstruct the emotional and stylistic rhythm of original works.

book:13503979.description: The Finnegans Wake Notebook Edition is a fully integrated and cross-referenced edition of all the extant work-books compiled by Joyce after the completion of Ulysses. It will be published as a series of fascicles, one per authorial notebook, three per scribal notebook, fifty-five in all. This will make individual notebooks available to scholars as they appear and allow critical feedback, laying the foundations for an electronic edition that will be prepared simultaneously. The editorial aim is to bring toge...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Joyce's work as a key example of culturally embedded text requiring radical translational adaptation.
Umberto Eco references Finnegans Wake as the source text embodying linguistic fragmentation and multilingual play, central to Joyce's translational philosophy.
Umberto Eco cites Finnegans Wake to argue that its dense intertextuality demands an informed reading, distinguishing it from the accessible duality of double coding.

book:15956695.description: 'Ulysses', one of the greatest novels of the 20th century, has had a profound influence on modern fiction. In a series of episodes covering the course of a single day, 16 June 1904, the novel traces the movements of Leopold Bloom and Stephen Dedalus through the streets of Dublin.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Joyce's Ulysses as an example of spatial representation through detailed listing, linking it to the rhetorical concept of hypotyposis.
Umberto Eco references Joyce’s Ulysses to contrast double coding with deliberate allegorical structure, noting that Joyce provides clear cues for the dual reading.
Umberto Eco references Joyce's Ulysses as a controversial and poorly received work, criticizing its style and dismissing it as not a work of art.

book:web_72f93aa2.description: A collection of James Joyce's Italian writings, edited by Jacqueline Risset, including texts produced in collaboration with Nino Frank, originally published in 1979 by Mondadori in Milan. The volume compiles Joyce's journalistic and literary pieces written in Italian, primarily from the 1930s.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this collected edition of Joyce's Italian writings as a source for historical translation variants of 'Anna Livia Plurabella'.

book:103800.description: Portrays Stephen Dedalus' Dublin childhood and youth, his quest for identity through art and his gradual emancipation from the claims of family, religion and Ireland itself.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Joyce's earlier novel to support the claim that his literary style deteriorates into incoherence and fragmentation.
Umberto Eco cites Joyce's novel as the starting point of his perceived artistic decline and rejection of national spirit.

Umberto Eco references Joyce's novel to illustrate Aristotle's conception of God as detached and transcendent, using the literary image to reinforce a philosophical argument about divine immanence and distance.
Umberto Eco lists this novel as a published work, indicating it is referenced as a literary source.
Umberto Eco references Joyce’s novel to illustrate the momentary illumination of beauty and its isolating effect on the individual.
Umberto Eco cites Joyce's novel as a source for a quoted passage used in a comparative table.

book:997958.description: Stephen Hero is a posthumously-published autobiographical novel by Irish author James Joyce. Its published form reflects only a portion of an original manuscript, part of which was lost. Many of its ideas were used in composing A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Joyce's Stephen Hero to define epiphany as a spiritual moment, and notes its recurring fiery imagery in Joyce’s works as an extension of D’Annunzio’s aesthetic fire.

book:web_61847250.description: An influential essay by Spanish philosopher José Ortega y Gasset on the challenges and paradoxes of translation, originally published in Volume V of his Obras completas by Revista de Occidente in 1947.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Ortega y Gasset’s essay as a key source in translation theory, noting its inclusion in a major anthology, implying its foundational role in the field.

book:119561.description:
Librarian note: an alternate cover for this edition can be found .
With vast erudition, Foucault cuts across disciplines and reaches back into seventeenth century to show how classical systems of knowledge, which linked all of nature within a great chain of being and analogies between the stars in the heavens and the features in a human face, gave way to the modern sciences of biology, philology, and political economy. The result is nothing less than an archaeology of the sciences that unearths old pattern...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Foucault's book as a canonical example of modern ekphrasis, highlighting its descriptive power in translating visual art into verbal text.

book:web_cfd24d28.description: The final book of the New Testament in the Christian Bible, traditionally attributed to John of Patmos, often identified with John the Apostle. It contains apocalyptic visions and symbolic imagery, including the throne in heaven described in chapter 4.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references St John’s Book of Revelation as the original biblical text that the illuminators struggled to visually translate, noting its hypotyposis and ambiguity.

book:8058415.description: Rene Descartes is perhaps most remembered for declaring, I think; therefore, I am. First published in 1644, Descartes s "Principles of Philosophy" elucidates the meaning of those words that ushered in a new era of philosophical thought. Unlike the medieval philosophers who often began by examining the existence and nature of God in a spirit of faith, Descartes begins by reflecting upon himself as one who doubts but who nonetheless desires certain knowledge of God and the world. In setting forth the truths h...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Descartes’ work to illustrate a compromise hypothesis that reconciled heliocentrism with church doctrine through the mechanism of celestial vortexes.

book:17027457.description:
"Le avventure di Pinocchio : storia di un burattino", nasce come racconto settimanale sul "Giornale dei bambini" nel 1881. Nel 1883 viene raccolto in volume.
Originariamente le avventure di Pinocchio si concludevano nell'episodio dell'impiccagione, con la morte del burattino. Le proteste dei piccoli lettori del "Giornale dei bambini" indussero pero l'autore a proseguire il racconto, che si concluse definitivamente, con la trasformazione del burattino in bambino, nel 1883.
Il capolavoro di Collodi e una stor...
commentaries: Umberto Eco analyzes Collodi's opening lines to illustrate a metafictional narrative strategy, contrasting it with translations and adaptations that alter its intended structure.
Umberto Eco references Collodi as the original author of Pinocchio to contrast the fidelity expected in literary translation with the freedom permitted in cinematic adaptation.
Umberto Eco includes Pinocchio as a secular mythic figure, citing Collodi’s original tale as the foundational text that established the character’s fluctuating yet identifiable properties.
Umberto Eco references this foundational semiotic text, presumably to align with its structuralist approach to language, though no direct argument from it is developed in the passage.

book:web_1e64e3b7.description: A cultural history of vagabonds and marginalized figures in Renaissance and early modern Italy, written by the renowned Italian scholar Piero Camporesi. The book explores the lives, representations, and social roles of beggars, pilgrims, and wanderers in Italian popular culture.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this book as the source for the obscure names of vagabonds used in The Name of the Rose, valuing its erudition and evocative power.

book:web_44d09494.description: A short letter written by Martin Luther in 1530 on the art and challenges of Bible translation, advocating for translating into vernacular German in a way that is accessible to ordinary people. It is a foundational text in translation theory.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Luther’s original 1530 letter on translation, citing its English translation within an edited volume.

book:6012840.description: Don Quixotehas become so entranced by reading chivalric romances, that he determines to become a knight-errant himself. In the company of his faithful squire, Sancho Panza, his exploits blossom in all sorts of wonderful ways. While Quixote's fancy often leads him astray - he tilts at windmills, imagining them to be giants - Sancho acquires cunning and a certain sagacity. Sane madman and wise fool, they roam the world together, and together they have haunted readers' imaginations for nearly four hundred year...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Cervantes’s Don Quixote as the original text reimagined by Menard, using it to exemplify intertextual irony through rewritten authorship.

book:web_0f09a000.description: A prose-verse work by Dante Alighieri, combining poetry and commentary to explore his love for Beatrice Portinari. It is considered a precursor to the Divine Comedy and a foundational text of Italian literature.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this edition of Dante’s Vita Nuova as a specific translated text used in discussion of translation practices.

book:18485642.description:
Dante Alighieri's epic poem, The Divine Comedy, is considered one of the finest works in Western Civilization. This edition is translated by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.
A table of contents is included.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Dante’s Divine Comedy as a text with prescribed multiple interpretive levels (literal, allegorical, moral), distinguishing it from postmodern double coding by emphasizing Umberto Eco’s intended didacticism.

Umberto Eco references Dante’s The Divine Comedy, particularly the Paradiso, as the pinnacle of medieval cosmological imagery of divine light and fire, noting its artistic influence and theological depth.
Umberto Eco cites Dante’s epic poem as a foundational text, referencing the original author despite the translation.
Umberto Eco references Dante's Divine Comedy as a significant literary and philosophical source, particularly in discussions of structure, symbolism, or moral vision.

book:web_8227e169.description: A collection of translations and essays by Dante Alighieri and other early Italian poets, originally published in 1861 by William Michael Rossetti. The 1908 edition by Ellis is a revised or reissued version titled 'Dante and His Circle with the Italian Poets Preceding Him'.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references this work as a scholarly compilation of Dante and earlier Italian poets, noting its original 1861 title.

book:19177.description: The Paradise, which Dante called the sublime canticle, is perhaps the most ambitious book of The Divine Comedy. In this climactic segment, Dante's pilgrim reaches Paradise and encounters the Divine Will. The poet's mystical interpretation of the religious life is a complex and exquisite conclusion to his magnificent trilogy. Mark Musa's powerful and sensitive translation preserves the intricacy of the work while rendering it in clear, rhythmic English. His extensive notes and introductions to each canto mak...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Dante's Paradise as a foundational example of poetic inadequacy in confronting the Divine, highlighting how Dante turns the impossibility of expression into the very subject of poetry.
Umberto Eco cites Dante's Paradise again to link faith with the acceptance of the Absolute's ineffability, framing faith as an epistemic substitute for knowledge.
Umberto Eco cites Dante’s Paradiso as a central text for medieval conceptions of divine light and spiritual ascent.

book:17465784.description: On a divine journey through the depths of Hell, Dante--with his guide, the poet Virgil--witnesses the fate of Earth's sinners. Inferno, a 14th century poem and the first part of Dante Alighieri's The Divine Comedy, paints an allegorical underworld in which sinners are punished in accordance with their sins. Journey through the darkness and meet famous historical and mythical figures and the fate that has become them, from Homer and Julius Caesar who dwell in Limbo with the unbaptized and the virtuous pagans...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Dante’s Inferno as a primary literary and symbolic source, particularly in discussions of generational conflict, moral hierarchy, or the afterlife.
Umberto Eco cites Dante’s treatise to illustrate his self-conception as a linguistic innovator who sought to restore a primordial, perfect language, positioning himself as a new Adam.
Umberto Eco cites this work by Dante as a referenced text, likely in the context of linguistic or philosophical inquiry.

book:208472.description:
Now I shall sing the second kingdom,
there where the soul of man is cleansed,
made worthy to ascend to heaven.
In the second book of Dante's epic poem The Divine Comedy, Dante has left hell and begins the ascent of the mount of purgatory. Just as hell had its circles, purgatory, situated at the threshold of heaven, has its terraces, each representing one of the seven mortal sins. With Virgil again as his guide, Dante climbs the mountain; the poet shows us, on its slopes, those whose lives were variously gov...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Dante's Purgatorio as a source for an English translation used in the text.

book:3295506.description: Quintilian was born in Spain about A.D. 35; he became a well-known and prosperous teacher of rhetoric in Rome, probably the first to receive a salary as such from public funds. His "Institutio Oratoria" ("Training of an Orator"), a comprehensive training program in twelve books, draws on his own rich experience. Here Quintilian gives guidelines for proper schooling (beginning with the young boy); analyzes the structure of speeches and recommends devices for engaging listeners and appealing to their emotions...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria to validate a rhetorical technique for creating visual impact through rhythmic, exaggerated event accumulation.

book:web_f2b4b49a.description: A collection of lyric poetry by Italian Baroque poet Giambattista Marino, first published in 1623. It is renowned for its elaborate metaphors, sensuous imagery, and influence on the Marinist poetic style.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Marino's La lira to illustrate how aesthetic ideals in poetry valorize deviation from conventional beauty, such as the allure of pallor in illness.

book:web_ab3fb505.description: A theological commentary on the Book of Revelation written by the Spanish monk Beatus of Liébana in the 8th century. It became highly influential in medieval Spain and is renowned for its richly illuminated manuscripts.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Beatus de Liébana's Commentary as the textual source that the Mozarabic illuminators attempted to illustrate in the Beati manuscripts.

book:web_c50e0d27.description: A groundbreaking collection of poetry by Charles Baudelaire, first published in 1857, which includes the poem 'Une Charogne' (The Carcass), known for its vivid and shocking imagery of decay and beauty.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Baudelaire's poem as a foundational text in the aestheticization of horror and decay, linking it to the rise of a religion of beauty rooted in the horrendous.
Umberto Eco uses Rabelais’s Gargantua as a prime example of rhythmic hypotyposis, where verbal cadence creates a vivid visual effect beyond mere listing.

book:web_6388a4bf.description: A medieval Latin treatise on poetry and rhetoric written by John of Garland, offering guidelines for composing verse, including definitions of poetic genres such as tragedy. It was influential in medieval literary education.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites John of Garland's Poetria Nova to illustrate medieval reinterpretations of tragedy, showing how the genre was redefined in terms of narrative structure rather than theatrical form.

book:web_a7196690.description: A prophetic book in the Hebrew Bible and Christian Old Testament, attributed to the prophet Ezekiel, who lived during the Babylonian exile. It contains visions, symbolic actions, and messages of judgment and restoration.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Ezekiel’s prophetic vision as the earlier textual source that influenced St John’s imagery and which the illuminators used to interpret the apocalyptic creatures, though unsuccessfully.

book:web_c9ade875.description: A seminal work by German philologist Ernst Robert Curtius, originally published in German in 1948 as 'Europäische Literatur und lateinisches Mittelalter'. It explores the continuity of Latin literary traditions in European literature from antiquity through the Middle Ages, emphasizing intertextuality and the persistence of classical motifs.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Curtius's book as the source that inspired his own use of medieval Latin quotations, acknowledging its influence on his intertextual approach.

book:web_21f28a5c.description: A 1891 interview published in Jules Huret's book 'Enquête sur l'évolution littéraire', in which Stéphane Mallarmé articulates his radical views on poetry, emphasizing suggestion over direct description and the power of silence and absence in literary expression.
commentaries: Umberto Eco uses Mallarmé’s essay to underscore the aesthetic principle that suggestion, not direct naming, constitutes the essence of poetic power.

book:3537012.description: Many chronicles have been written about life at sea, but few, if any, can compare with Joseph Conrad's masterpiece. It is the story of one unremarkable steamship captain, pitted against a storm of incredible fury. Captain Macwhirr has a reputation as a solid, steadfast man, who "having just enough imagination to carry him through each successive day, and no more" cannot fully believe any storm would be a match for his powerful ship. So, when the barometer and other clues begin to hint at trouble ahead, he i...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Conrad's original work through Gide's French translation to illustrate challenges in translating idiomatic expressions and the tension between foreignising and domesticating strategies.

book:web_3e552edc.description: A seminal work in translation studies by French translator and theorist Antoine Berman, exploring the ethical and aesthetic dimensions of translation, particularly the tension between fidelity to the letter of the source text and the demands of the target culture. The second edition (1999) is the most widely cited version.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Berman’s book as a source of theoretical framing, with a direct quote from another work embedded within it.

book:7105277.description: This groundbreaking English version by Robert Fagles is the most important recent translation of Homer's great epic poem. The verse translation has been hailed by scholars as the new standard, providing an Iliad that delights modern sensibility and aesthetic without sacrificing the grandeur and particular genius of Homer's own style and language. The Iliad is one of the two great epics of Homer, and is typically described as one of the greatest war stories of all time, but to say the Iliad is a war story do...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Homer's Iliad as a classical example of spatial description through cataloguing, using it to illustrate a literary technique relevant to hypotyposis.
Umberto Eco cites Homer’s Iliad as an ancient literary prototype for the scapegoating of socially marginalized figures, drawing a parallel between Thersites and later antisemitic caricatures.
Umberto Eco references Homer’s Iliad as a classical source for themes of heroism, violence, or aesthetics, without specifying a translated edition.

book:9459566.description: This is an EXACT reproduction of a book published before 1923. This IS NOT an OCR'd book with strange characters, introduced typographical errors, and jumbled words. This book may have occasional imperfections such as missing or blurred pages, poor pictures, errant marks, etc. that were either part of the original artifact, or were introduced by the scanning process. We believe this work is culturally important, and despite the imperfections, have elected to bring it back into print as part of our continuin...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Virgil's Georgica as a key literary example demonstrating the fluid and context-dependent use of the Latin colour term glaucus, illustrating how colour terminology in classical literature resists fixed categorization.

book:337463.description: The story is about a hero's love for three women, all of whom he loses; a hymn to unattainable, unrequited love. The story begins when a paragraph in a newspaper plunges the narrator into his memories as a younger man. The perspective seems to shift back and forth between the past and present, so the reader is never entirely sure if the narrator is recounting past events from memory, or retelling current events as they happen. Critics have praised the writing for its lucid and lyrical style. The narrator, o...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Gérard de Nerval's 'Sylvie' as one of two works he translated, emphasizing the labor-intensive nature of his translation practice.
Umberto Eco references Nerval’s Sylvie as a text he himself translated, comparing his approach with those of other English translators.

book:3473246.description: Apparso in "Letteratura" nell'immediato dopoguerra, inizialmente letto e ammirato da pochi, il "Pasticciaccio" fu scritto a Firenze nel ricordo lontano di soggiorni romani, ma come rinverditi da quotidiane immersioni nella lettura del Belli e intessuto su un reale fatto di sangue. L'intrigo poliziesco che ne deriva si giustifica in duplice direzione: eco del mondo e bricolage letterario. Il fascismo, la morte, il lenocinio, il furto, le bassezze degli uomini, tutte metafore di un male oscuro, conducono il l...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Gadda's novel as a work whose linguistic complexity cannot be captured in film, underscoring the irreplaceable value of the original text in translation.

book:web_304819ea.description: A guide on writing radio scripts by Italian writer Carlo Emilio Gadda, first published anonymously in 1953 by Edizioni Radio italiana, then expanded and republished under his name in 1973 by ERI—Edizioni Rai Radiotelevisione italiana.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Gadda's work as a foundational text on radio script formatting, noting its two editions.
Umberto Eco cites Melville's Moby Dick to illustrate the impropriety of citing the location of a recent edition as the place of publication.

book:web_94eeaf1f.description: A seminal survey of Italian literature from the 19th to the 20th century by the renowned Italian philologist and literary critic Gianfranco Contini, first published in 1957. It is a foundational critical work in the study of modern Italian literature.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Contini's survey as an example of a scholarly work that, while comprehensive and intentional in its omissions, would be inappropriate as a student thesis due to its scope and the risk of misinterpretation.

book:1018951.description: Five Union prisoners escape from the seige of Richmond in a balloon, are blown off course and crash on an uncharted island. They must learn to rebuild a society for themselves while awaiting rescue.
commentaries: Verne's novel is cited as an example of a foreign text translated into other languages, used to explore the dynamics of source-text fidelity and target-language adaptation.

book:web_13f33ed4.description: A collection of anecdotes, quotations, and discussions on grammar, philosophy, history, and antiquities by the Roman author Aulus Gellius, written in the 2nd century AD. The work is organized into twenty books and is a key source for understanding Roman intellectual life.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Aulus Gellius’s ancient text as a concrete example of historical challenges in interpreting color terminology, highlighting the limits of linguistic and perceptual reconstruction across time.

book:web_55e545fd.description: A foundational reference work in semiotics, co-edited by Algirdas J. Greimas and Joseph Courtés, offering analytical entries on key terms in structural semiotics and linguistic theory. Published by Indiana University Press in 1982, it systematized the semiotic framework developed by the Paris School.
commentaries: Umberto Eco alludes to this dictionary as a reference tool for semiotic terminology, suggesting its utility in analyzing translation phenomena without quoting or expanding on its content.

book:566328.description: Set in Lombardy during the Spanish occupation of the late 1620s, The Betrothed tells the story of two young lovers, Renzo and Lucia, prevented from marrying by the petty tyrant Don Rodrigo, who desires Lucia for himself. Forced to flee, they are then cruelly separated, and must face many dangers including plague, famine and imprisonment, and confront a variety of strange characters - the mysterious Nun of Monza, the fiery Father Cristoforo and the sinister 'Unnamed' - in their struggle to be reunited. A vig...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Manzoni's novel to demonstrate how subtle, minimal language in literature can convey complex meaning without explicit detail, contrasting it with the necessary explicitness of film adaptation.
Umberto Eco cites Manzoni’s novel as a well-known literary source whose phrasing is recognizable and should be mirrored in translation through equivalent literary allusions.
Umberto Eco contrasts personal knowledge of a real parent with complete textual knowledge of Manzoni’s fictional character, arguing for the ontological clarity of literary figures.
Umberto Eco uses Manzoni's novel as an example to illustrate the fallacy of equating an author with a single work.

Umberto Eco cites Manzoni’s I promessi sposi as a narrative model for understanding shifting actant roles, using it to illustrate how characters can embody changing narrative functions within a story’s structure.

book:6643457.description: Carlo, re dei Franchi, ha ripudiato Ermengarda, figlia di Desiderio, re dei Longobardi. Ermengarda torna dal padre e chiede di potersi chiudere in convento per trovare conforto nella preghiera. Un messo di Carlo intima a Desiderio di restituire le terre tolte al pontefice. Il re risponde sdegnosamente e la guerra e dichiarata. Alcuni duchi longobardi sono pronti a tradire. Nel campo dei Franchi giunge il diacono Martino a rivelare l'esistenza di un valico che permette a Carlo di prendere di sorpresa i Longo...
commentaries: Umberto Eco contrasts two of Manzoni’s works to argue that an author’s identity cannot be reduced to any single text.

book:241061.description:
This timely reissue of Richard Hofstadter's classic work on the fringe groups that influence American electoral politics offers an invaluable perspective on contemporary domestic affairs.
In The Paranoid Style in American Politics, acclaimed historian Richard Hofstadter examines the competing forces in American political discourse and how fringe groups can influence -- and derail -- the larger agendas of a political party. He investigates the politics of the irrational, shedding light on how the behavior of...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Hofstadter's book as a foundational text for understanding conspiracy thinking through a psychological lens.

book:765346.description: First published in 1967, Writing and Difference, a collection of Jacques Derrida's essays written between 1959 and 1966, has become a landmark of contemporary French thought. In it we find Derrida at work on his systematic deconstruction of Western metaphysics. The book's first half, which includes the celebrated essay on Descartes and Foucault, shows the development of Derrida's method of deconstruction. In these essays, Derrida demonstrates the traditional nature of some purportedly nontraditional current...
commentaries: Umberto Eco quotes Derrida to illustrate the paradoxical nature of translation—its necessary loss of the original's physical substance—using this passage as a critical touchstone.

book:web_75816b87.description: A polemical treatise by Saint Jerome against the views of Jovinian, who promoted the equality of married and celibate Christian life. Written in 393 AD, it is one of Jerome's most controversial works, defending asceticism and virginity.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Saint Jerome's work as a vivid example of classical disapproval of stylistic excess, using it to contrast with later Hisperic poetic practices.
Umberto Eco cites this encyclical to illustrate the Church’s concern that modern philosophy’s focus on epistemic limits fosters relativism and skepticism, undermining the pursuit of objective truth.
Umberto Eco cites this encyclical to illustrate the Church’s concern that modern philosophy’s focus on epistemological limits has fostered relativism and skepticism.
Umberto Eco cites this papal encyclical as a doctrinal source on faith and reason, referencing the original author.

book:web_dd16934d.description: Italian psychologist and historian Giovanni Jervis, known for his work in social psychology and critical analysis of contemporary thought, published 'Contro il relativismo' in 2005 as a critique of relativist ideologies in modern culture, particularly targeting postmodern and New Age trends.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Jervis's book to illustrate a caricatured version of relativism used to critique its perceived irrationality and reactionary tendencies in cultural anthropology.
Umberto Eco cites Jervis’s book as a critique of a distorted form of relativism, portraying it as anti-scientific and ideologically reactionary.
Umberto Eco lists this book as a published work, indicating it is referenced as a source on relativism.

book:web_7fd7ecdd.description: A treatise by the Byzantine scholar Michael Psellos, written in the 11th century, addressing demonic activity, superstition, and heretical practices in Byzantine society. It reflects contemporary theological and philosophical debates about magic, demons, and religious deviance.
commentaries: Umberto Eco uses Psello’s medieval text to illustrate the historical roots of blood libel and demonization of Jews as ritual murderers and heretics within Christian thought.

book:16081905.description:
Cuore e un libro per ragazzi a episodi separati, scritto da Edmondo de Amicis a Torino e pubblicato, per la prima volta, dalla casa editrice milanese Treves nel 1886.
Fu un grande successo, tanto che de Amicis divenne lo scrittore piu letto d'Italia. L'ambientazione e la Torino dell'Unita d'Italia, e piu precisamente tra il 1878 (anno d'incoronazione del Re Umberto I) ed il 1886 (anno della pubblicazione del libro), e il testo ha il chiaro scopo di insegnare ai giovani cittadini del Regno le virtu civili, o...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Amicis’s Cuore to show how the literary portrayal of a morally repugnant child—Franti—functions as a modern secular analog to ancient scapegoating figures like Thersites.

book:web_29e46548.description: A 1964 study by Italian art historians Giuseppina and Eugenio Battisti on the cultural and historical representation of witches in early modern Europe, particularly focusing on folklore, trial records, and iconography.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references the Battistis’ work as a source for a specific trial transcript, using it to draw parallels between witchcraft and Templar trials.

book:web_95efdfab.description: A medieval manual for inquisitors written by Bernardo Gui, a Dominican friar and inquisitor in Languedoc, providing detailed procedures for identifying, interrogating, and prosecuting heretics during the Inquisition. It is one of the earliest and most influential guides for inquisitorial practice in the 14th century.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Gui’s manual as one of the earliest inquisitorial texts that helped institutionalize the persecution of heretics.

book:web_ac031f99.description: A two-volume critical study by French literary critic Alfred Nettement, examining the popular serialized novels (feuilletons) of the 19th century. Published in 1845, it is one of the earliest substantial critical analyses of this form of mass literature.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Alfred Nettement's scholarly work as a key historical critique of the serialized novel, using it to validate the genre’s cultural controversy.
Umberto Eco cites Frankenstein as a pivotal text in which ugliness becomes a vehicle for empathy and moral reflection.
Umberto Eco lists this novel as a published work, indicating it is referenced as a literary source.
Umberto Eco cites Shelley’s novel as a touchstone for discussions of creation, hubris, and the boundaries of human knowledge.

book:221533.description: Counterfactualsis David Lewis' forceful presentation of and sustained argument for a particular view about propositions which express contrary to fact conditionals, including his famous defense of realism about possible worlds.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this philosophical text to draw a parallel between science fiction's multiverse tropes and analytic metaphysics' realist theory of possible worlds.

book:web_27b7fafb.description: A foundational text in criminology by Italian physician and psychiatrist Cesare Lombroso, proposing that criminal behavior is inherited and that criminals can be identified by physical traits. The first volume was published in 1876.
