commentaries: Umberto Eco references Lombroso’s criminological work to support a pseudoscientific claim linking Romani people to foul odor through alleged dietary habits.

book:1140653.description: Cesare Lombroso is widely considered the founder of criminology. His theory of the "born" criminal dominated European and American thinking about the causes of criminal behavior during the late nineteenth century and the early twentieth. This volume offers English-language readers the first critical, scholarly translation of Lombroso's Criminal Man, one of the most famous criminological treatises ever written. The text laid the groundwork for subsequent biological theories of crime, including contemporary g...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Lombroso’s criminological work as the scientific culmination of physiognomic theories linking physical appearance to moral character.
Umberto Eco cites Lombroso’s work as a key source on criminal physiognomy, linking physical appearance to moral or criminal traits.

book:web_97ad2d55.description: A 17th-century French utopian novel by Gabriel de Foigny, describing a fictional southern continent inhabited by a race of androgynous, rational beings. It was published in Geneva and became a notable work of early speculative fiction.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Foigny’s Terra Australis as one of the early modern imagined islands representing perfect, unknown civilizations.

book:25678.description:
"Men like Benvenuto, unique in their profession, need not be subject to the law."
--Pope Paul III on learning that Cellini had murdered a fellow artist
Benvenuto Cellini was beloved in Renaissance Florence. A renowned sculptor and goldsmith whose works include the famous salt-cellar made for the King of France, and the statue of Perseus with the head of the Medusa, Cellini's life was as vivid and enthralling as his creations. A man of action as well as an artist, he took part in the Sack of Rome in 1527; he...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Cellini's autobiography as a concrete example of fire as an artistic instrument in sculpture, highlighting the alchemical parallels in artistic creation.
Umberto Eco cites Cellini's autobiography as a source of insight into personal narrative and self-representation in the Renaissance.

book:web_3c357f1a.description: A collection of moral and theological discourses by Odo of Cluny, a prominent 10th-century Benedictine abbot and reformer. The 'Collationes' (also known as 'Dialogus de virtutibus et vitiis') consists of conversations on Christian ethics, asceticism, and the nature of sin, often employing vivid and harsh imagery to critique worldly pleasures and the human body. The cited passage reflects Odo's ascetic worldview, common in monastic literature of the period.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Odo of Cluny's Collationes to demonstrate medieval theological misogyny, using it as evidence of how religious thought framed women's bodies as inherently repulsive and spiritually dangerous.

book:25709.description: Creating a summary of all human knowledge may not be the sort of undertaking we begin in the twenty-first century, but there is still room on our bookshelves for a classic--Summa Theologica, one of the world's oldest and greatest masterpieces. St. Thomas Aquinas has much to teach us--most especially how to confront the classic questions that are still with us after centuries of thought.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Aquinas’s Summa Theologica to explain the medieval theological resolution of how original sin is transmitted without material soul transmission.
Umberto Eco cites Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologica as a primary source for medieval theological reasoning on the infusion of the rational soul.
Umberto Eco references the Supplement to the Summa Theologica, attributing it to Reginald of Piperno, to explore medieval views on bodily resurrection and the status of the embryo.
Umberto Eco cites the Summa as a primary source for Thomas Aquinas’s doctrine on the staged infusion of the soul during fetal development.
Umberto Eco references the Summa to support Thomas Aquinas’s distinction between the sensitive soul in the embryo and the later infusion of the rational soul.
Umberto Eco cites the Summa to illustrate Thomas Aquinas’s view that the sensitive soul arises from the active power in semen, not through material transmission.
Umberto Eco uses the Summa to highlight Thomas Aquinas’s argument that the intellective soul cannot be generated by natural means but must be created by God.

book:2342655.description: The Summa Contra Gentilesis not merely the only complete summary of Christian doctrine that St. Thomas has written, but also a creative and even revolutionary work of Christian apologetics composed at the precise moment when Christian thought needed to be intellectually creative in order to master and assimilate the intelligence and wisdom of the Greeks and the Arabs. In the Summa, Aquinas works to save and purify the thought of the Greeks and the Arabs in the higher light of Christian Revelation, confident...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Summa contra Gentiles to reinforce Thomas Aquinas’s hierarchical model of soul development in fetal formation.

book:web_bd9b7a5f.description: Thomas Aquinas's early theological commentary on Peter Lombard's 'Sentences', written around 1252–1256, which includes detailed distinctions on theological and philosophical topics, including causality.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references this medieval theological text to show how pre-scientific cosmological models anticipate later scientific reconsiderations, such as cold fusion.
Umberto Eco cites Aquinas's Summa theologiae as a key medieval source distinguishing types of lies by moral severity, using specific theological references to support the analysis.
Umberto Eco cites this theological compendium as a primary source, referencing its original author despite the translated edition.

book:964338.description: Ostensibly written by an English knight, the Travels purport to relate his experiences in the Holy Land, Egypt, India and China. Mandeville claims to have served in the Great Khan's army, and to have travelled in 'the lands beyond' - countries populated by dog-headed men, cannibals, Amazons and Pygmies. Although Marco Polo's slightly earlier narrative ultimately proved more factually accurate, Mandeville's was widely known, used by Columbus, Leonardo da Vinci and Martin Frobisher, and inspiring writers as d...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Mandeville’s Travels as a key medieval source that conflates Ceylon and Taprobane, using its vivid descriptions to explore the blurring of real and imagined geography.

book:web_82ac875b.description: A medieval astronomical treatise by John of Holywood (also known as Johannes de Sacrobosco), based on Ptolemaic cosmology. It became the standard textbook on the sphere of the world in European universities from the 13th to the 17th century.
commentaries: Umberto Eco presents John of Holywood’s tract as the dominant medieval textbook on the sphere of the world, grounded in Ptolemaic astronomy.

book:web_09febcc3.description: A philosophical and occult treatise by the Italian Dominican friar and philosopher Tommaso Campanella, exploring the nature of sensory perception and magic within a naturalistic and hermetic framework. Written during his imprisonment, it reflects his syncretic blend of Aristotelianism, Neoplatonism, and Renaissance magic.
commentaries: Umberto Eco notes that Camporesi draws on Campanella’s De sensu rerum et magia as a source for historical beliefs about cheese, integrating it into a broader textual collage of medieval and early modern views.

book:web_f7adc497.description: A seminal 16th-century Spanish navigational manual by Pedro de Medina, widely used by Portuguese and Spanish sailors. It covered cartography, astronomy, and practical seamanship, and was one of the most influential navigation texts of the Age of Exploration.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Pedro da Medina's Arte del navegar as a navigational text that includes the mythical island of Antillia, illustrating how cartographic confusion persisted in Renaissance maritime literature.

book:2171496.description: Travel to other planets is a reality, and with overpopulation stretching the resources of Earth, the necessity to find habitable worlds is growing ever more urgent. With no time to wait years for communication between slower-than-light spaceships and home, the Long Range Foundation explores an unlikely solution--human telepathy. Identical twins Tom and Pat are enlisted to be the human radios that will keep the ships in contact with Earth, but one of them has to stay behind while the other explores the depth...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this novel as an example of science fiction exploring relativistic time effects and telepathic communication in space travel.

book:12769646.description: From the First Golden Age of SF master Robert A. Heinlein, this is the so-called juvenile (written, Heinlein always claims, just as much for adults) that started them all and made Heinlein a legend for multiple generations of readers. A poor young man seeks his fortune in space and comes of age a ship's officer and hero.The stars were closed to Max Jones. To get into space you either needed connections, a membership in the Guild, or a whole lot more money than Max, the son of a widowed, poor mother, was eve...
commentaries: Umberto Eco uses this passage to illustrate how science fiction employs intuitive analogies to conceptualize hyperspace and non-Euclidean navigation.

book:1698318.description: It is 1970, and electronics engineer Dan Davis has finally made the invention of a lifetime: a household robot with extraordinary abilities, destined to dramatically change the landscape of everyday routine. Then, with wild success just within reach, Dan's greedy partner and even greedier fiancee steal his work and leave him penniless, and trick him into taking the long sleep--suspended animation for thirty years.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Heinlein’s novel alongside other science fiction works as a source of ideas on possible worlds, indicating its role in shaping the thesis structure.

book:web_08ce7074.description: A two-volume work by English physician and occult philosopher Robert Fludd, presenting a syncretic cosmology blending Hermeticism, Christian mysticism, and Renaissance science. The first volume (1617) deals with the macrocosm (the universe), and the second (1621) with the microcosm (the human being). It includes elaborate engravings and defends a traditional, hierarchical view of the cosmos against emerging Copernican ideas.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Fludd’s work as an example of mechanical objections to heliocentrism, using it to demonstrate how contemporary scholars defended geocentrism with physical reasoning.

book:7051295.description: Wilhelm Richard Wagner (1813-1883) was a German composer, conductor, music theorist, and essayist, primarily known for his operas (later called music dramas). Wagners musical style is often considered the epitome of classical musics Romantic period, due to its unprecedented exploration of emotional expression. He transformed musical thought through his idea of Gesamtkunstwerk (total artwork), the synthesis of all the poetic, visual, musical and dramatic arts, epitomized by his monumental four-opera cycle Th...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Wagner’s essay as a key ideological source linking Jewish identity with artistic incapacity and aesthetic repulsiveness, particularly in music.
Umberto Eco cites Wagner's 'Judaism in Music' as an example of anti-Semitic rhetoric in 19th-century thought.
Umberto Eco cites Wagner’s essay as a published work, referencing the original author despite the translation.

book:web_9bd7498f.description: A 17th-century scholarly work by Jesuit polymath Athanasius Kircher that uses physics and mathematics to argue that the Tower of Babel could not have reached heaven, blending theology, linguistics, and early scientific reasoning.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Kircher's Turris Babel as an instance of applying mathematical reasoning to a biblical narrative, revealing the intersection of science and myth in early modern thought.

book:web_bcda30c8.description: A 1660 cosmological work by Jesuit scholar Athanasius Kircher, presenting various models of the solar system, including the Copernican system, alongside mythological and ancient systems. It reflects the scientific and theological tensions of the 17th century.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Kircher’s book to illustrate the tension between traditional and emerging cosmological models, highlighting Kircher’s rejection of Copernicanism despite his detailed presentation of it.

book:web_aa1f624b.description: A comprehensive 17th-century work by Jesuit scholar Athanasius Kircher on the hidden structures and phenomena of the Earth, including volcanoes, fossils, and subterranean waters. It blends scientific observation with speculative natural philosophy.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Kircher's work as an example of pre-scientific but earnest attempts to explain natural phenomena through observation and imaginative theory.

book:168542.description: Cicero (Marcus Tullius, 10643 BCE), Roman lawyer, orator, politician and philosopher, of whom we know more than of any other Roman, lived through the stirring era which saw the rise, dictatorship, and death of Julius Caesar in a tottering republic. In his political speeches especially and in his correspondence we see the excitement, tension and intrigue of politics and the part he played in the turmoil of the time. Of about 106 speeches, delivered before the Roman people or the Senate if they were political...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Cicero's orations as a historical example of constructing an enemy through moralistic rhetoric, even when the threat was already established.
Umberto Eco references Pseudo-Dionysius's Celestial Hierarchy to illustrate the use of negative theology and metaphorical language in approaching the ineffable Divine.
Umberto Eco cites this work to illustrate how divine reality is expressed through negative symbols and metaphorical language due to the limits of human expression.
Umberto Eco cites Pseudo-Dionysius’s Celestial Hierarchy as a key medieval text that uses fire as a symbol of divine transcendence and incorporeal light, directly quoting its theological imagery.

book:10427269.description: On the Divine Names is about a kind of divine name which describes multiple attributes of godhead as a whole. Tho the names refer to it as a unity, each name is different & so, taken together, they differentiate it. The implicit distinction between the godhead's unity & the multiplicity of the names is reflected in the names' structures themselves. Each includes a Greek prefix: hyper-, which indicates the unity of the godhead to whom names are applied. But each name is different, indicating the self-multipl...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this work as a source on theological or mystical concepts, likely relating to the nature of divinity and symbolism.
Umberto Eco cites Pseudo-Dionysius as a foundational source for negative theology and mystical tradition.

book:424055.description: The Metamorphosis, first published in 1915, is the most famous of Kafka's works, along with The Trial and The Castle. The story begins when a traveling salesman, Gregor Samsa, wakes up to find himself transformed into a giant insect. Curiously, his condition does not arouse surprise in his family, who merely despise it as an impending burden. As with all of Kafka's works, The Metamorphosis is open to a wide range of interpretations. Most obvious are themes relating to society's treatment of those who are di...
commentaries: Umberto Eco invokes Gregor Samsa from Kafka’s Metamorphosis to contrast the fixed fate of fictional characters with imagined alternatives, citing Kafka’s novella as the authoritative origin of the character’s transformation.

book:20501596.description:
Originally written in German, but the German manuscript was lost & only the manuscript of the English translation survived.
Darkness At Noonstands as an unequaled fictional portrayal of the nightmare politics of our time. Its hero is an aging revolutionary, imprisoned & psychologically tortured by the Party to which he has dedicated his life. As the pressure to confess preposterous crimes increases, he relives a career that embodies the terrible ironies & human betrayals of a totalitarian movement masking i...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Koestler’s novel as a literary parallel to the psychological mechanisms of forced confessions in both witch trials and Stalinist purges.

book:web_5d43ffb4.description: Joseph Ratzinger, later Pope Benedict XVI, contributed an essay to the 2002 volume 'Il monoteismo', edited by Giuseppe Ruggieri, which explores monotheism from theological, philosophical, and historical perspectives. Ratzinger's contribution reflects his views on truth, reason, and the uniqueness of the Christian God in contrast to modern relativism.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Ratzinger's contribution to this book to highlight his critique of modern epistemology, arguing that replacing truth with consensus undermines moral and metaphysical foundations.
Umberto Eco cites Ratzinger’s book to show his critique of modern scientific rationality as inherently relativistic, contrasting it with revealed theological truth.

book:22453611.description:
We have only to speak of an object to think that we are being objective. But, because we chose it in the first place, the object reveals more about us than we do about it. What we consider to be our fundamental ideas concerning the world are often indications of the immaturity of our minds.
Preface
Introduction
Fire & Respect
Fire & Reverie
Psychoanalysis & Prehistory
Sexualized Fire
The Chemistry of Fire
Alcohol
Idealized Fire
Conclusion
Footnotes
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Bachelard's book as a direct source for a poetic description of domestic fire, using it to ground the personal memory in a scholarly framework.

book:790967.description: Printed in the same size and format as the original, the book includes all the woodcuts and has a substantial introduction by Professor Godwin. Its appearance is a publishing event, filling a notorious gap in every academic library, in the collections of scholars, and on the bookshelves of everyone interested in the history of Western culture.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Hypnerotomachia Poliphili as a classic of linguistic corruption and a precursor to Joyce, suggesting its ornate and excessive language as a model for indulgent wordplay.

book:3406981.description: Saat di Paris, pakar simbologi Harvard, Robert Langdon, menerima telepon tengah malam yang penting. Seorang kurator senior di Museum Louvre terbunuh, dan pesan-pesan rahasia yang mengherankan ditemukan dekat tubuhnya. Ketika Langdon dan seorang kryptolog (pemecah kode) berbakat Prancis, Sophie Neveu, mengupas lapis demi lapis teka-teki aneh itu, mereka terpana menemukan serangkaian petunjuk tersembunyi di balik karya-karya terkenal Da Vinci - petunjuk-petunjuk yang tampak agar dilihat semua orang tapi senga...
commentaries: Umberto Eco identifies Dan Brown’s novel as a contemporary cultural manifestation of the conspiracy syndrome, noting its role in popularizing and legitimizing fictional conspiracies among the public.

book:web_8c704777.description: A chronicle written by the Burgundian monk Rodulfus Glaber, covering European history from 900 to 1044, notable for its vivid descriptions and apocalyptic tone, including accounts of Attila the Hun and other historical figures.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Rodolfus Glaber’s description of Attila to show how the enemy’s physical traits were merged with demonic imagery to reinforce moral and spiritual alienation.

book:web_10c40856.description: A 3rd-century Christian theological work by Hippolytus of Rome, also known as 'Refutation of All Heresies,' which critiques various heresies and includes philosophical discussions, including references to pre-Socratic thinkers like Democritus and atomism.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Hippolytus’ work as a historical source documenting early atomist theories about the plurality of worlds, linking them to later cosmological debates.

book:7520474.description: Through his highly idiosyncratic readings of some of the finest paintings, sculptures, and poems of the French and Italian Renaissance, Walter Pater in Studies in the History of the Renaissanceredefined the practice of criticism as an impressionistic, almost erotic exploration of the critic's aesthetic responses. Pater's infamous "Conclusion," which forever linked him with the decadent movement, scandalized many with its insistence on making pleasure the sole motive of life, even as it charmed fellow aesthe...
commentaries: Umberto Eco identifies Pater's The Renaissance as the origin of the concept of epiphany, linking it to fleeting aesthetic experiences and the metaphor of fire.
Umberto Eco cites Fontenelle’s book to trace the intellectual lineage of the plurality of worlds hypothesis from Cartesian physics to early science fiction.

book:web_5222e0b2.description: A collection of miscellaneous thoughts and observations by Italian poet and writer Alessandro Tassoni, published in 1627. The work includes skeptical and ironic reflections on scientific, philosophical, and cultural topics of the time, including critiques of Aristotelian cosmology.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Tassoni’s book as a source of anti-Copernican arguments, specifically quoting two of its objections to Earth’s motion.

book:45156.description: Sensational, dramatic, packed with rich excitement and filled with the sweep and violence of human passions, LES MISERABLES is not only superb adventure but a powerful social document. The story of how the convict Jean-Valjean struggled to escape his past and reaffirm his humanity, in a world brutalized by poverty and ignorance, became the gospel of the poor and the oppressed.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Hugo's Les misérables as the textual location where Hugo references Joseph de Maistre, using it to illustrate Hugo's complex justification of revolutionary violence through the lens of sacrifice and moral ambiguity.
Umberto Eco invokes this novel to contrast Hugo’s divine, omniscient narrative style with Stendhal’s limited perspective, highlighting Hugo’s use of historical events as metaphysical drama.

book:1971935.description: With a cast spanning the doomed aristocracy and the suffering peasantry and including the warring revolutionary leaders Marat, Danton and Robespierre, Hugo brings to life the year 1793 - the year of the guillotine
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Hugo's novel Ninety-three as a central example of stylistic excess used to convey historical and moral conflict, praising its emotional intensity and symbolic depth.

book:349376.description: Quasimodo, the hunchback bellringer of Notre-Dame Cathedral, is devoted to the beautiful gypsy dancer, La Esmerelda. When the demented archdeacon Frollo hatches a devilish plot to abduct La Esmerelda, Quasimodo will go to any lengths to protect the woman he loves.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this novel to illustrate Hugo’s recurring motif of symbolic conflict between old and new forces, using Frollo’s famous phrase as a parallel to the guillotine’s symbolic role in Ninety-three.

book:8522696.description: This is a reproduction of a book published before 1923. This book may have occasional imperfections such as missing or blurred pages, poor pictures, errant marks, etc. that were either part of the original artifact, or were introduced by the scanning process. We believe this work is culturally important, and despite the imperfections, have elected to bring it back into print as part of our continuing commitment to the preservation of printed works worldwide. We appreciate your understanding of the imperfect...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Hugo’s preface to Cromwell as the theoretical foundation for Hugo’s literary treatment of the grotesque, linking it to Romantic aesthetics and the redefinition of beauty.
Umberto Eco cites Hugo’s preface to 'Cromwell' as the foundational Romantic text redefining the sublime through ugliness.

book:63038.description: Victor Hugo's The Man Who Laughs(first published under the French title L'Homme qui Ritin April 1869) is a sad and sordid tale -- not the sort of tale of the moment Hugo was known for. It starts on the night of January 29, 1690, a ten-year-old boy abandoned -- the stern men who've kept him since infancy have wearied of him. The boy wanders, barefoot and starving, through a snowstorm to reach a gibbet bearing the corpse of a hanged criminal. Beneath the gibbet is a ragged woman, frozen to death. The boy is a...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites 'The Man who Laughs' as a literary embodiment of the aestheticization of deformity and its erotic and philosophical implications.

book:11381744.description: With accuracy, wit, and intelligence, this remarkable new translation of The Golden Assbreathes new life into Apuleius's classic work. Sarah Ruden, a lyric poet as well as a highly respected translator, skillfully duplicates the verbal high jinks of Apuleius's ever-popular novel. It tells the story of Lucius, a curious and silly young man, who is turned into a donkey when he meddles with witchcraft. Doomed to wander from region to region and mistreated by a series of deplorable owners, Lucius at last is res...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Apuleius’s The Golden Ass as one of the few classical literary sources depicting witches, using it to contrast ancient perceptions of witchcraft with later modern demonization.

book:4982.description: The Sirens of Titan is an outrageous romp through space, time, and morality. The richest, most depraved man on Earth, Malachi Constant, is offered a chance to take a space journey to distant worlds with a beautiful woman at his side. Of course there's a catch to the invitation--and a prophetic vision about the purpose of human life that only Vonnegut has the courage to tell.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this novel as an example of science fiction inventing speculative cosmological structures that echo real scientific hypotheses.

book:web_bcd49673.description: A devotional work by Saint Alphonsus Liguori, an Italian Catholic bishop, theologian, and Doctor of the Church, focusing on preparation for death and the final judgment. It is part of his extensive spiritual writings, widely read in Catholic tradition.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Saint Alphonsus de Liguori’s Apparecchio alla morte to exemplify the baroque intensification of hellfire imagery, emphasizing its physical and psychological torment.

book:web_75a8368d.description: A treatise on witchcraft and heresy written by the Dominican theologian John Nider between 1435 and 1437, and first published in 1473. It is one of the earliest systematic works on witchcraft in the early modern period, influencing later inquisitorial manuals such as the Malleus Maleficarum.
commentaries: Umberto Eco identifies Nider’s Formicarius as the first modern text to systematically describe witchcraft practices, later influencing the Malleus maleficarum.

book:22666067.description:
The author's biography is included in this version.
Flatland: A Romance of Many Dimensions is an 1884 satirical novella by the English schoolmaster Edwin Abbott Abbott. Writing pseudonymously as "a Square", Abbott used the fictional two-dimensional world of Flatland to offer pointed observations on the social hierarchy of Victorian culture. However, the novella's more enduring contribution is its examination of dimensions, for which the novella is still popular amongst mathematics, physics, and computer sci...
commentaries: Umberto Eco invokes Abbott's Flatland as a metaphor for limited perception, drawing a parallel between two-dimensional beings and navigators who can only see islands as silhouettes without full spatial context.
Umberto Eco cites Nietzsche's essay as the origin of the relativist claim that facts are merely interpretations, and uses it as a central reference point for critiquing modern relativism.
Umberto Eco identifies Nietzsche’s essay as the origin of the extreme relativist claim that all truth is interpretation, distinguishing it from moderate forms of relativism.
Umberto Eco cites Nietzsche’s essay as a critical source for understanding the constructed nature of truth and the ethics of deception.

book:451553.description:
Innehaller:
Otidsenliga betraktelser I-IV
Vi filologer
Om vara bildningsanstalters framtid
Fem foretal till fem oskrivna bocker
Om sanning och logn i utmmoralisk mening
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Nietzsche’s work as a foundational text, possibly for its critical engagement with culture and morality.

book:34033784.description: On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres is the seminal work on the heliocentric theory of the Renaissance astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus (1473-1543). The book, first printed in 1543 in Nuremberg, Holy Roman Empire, offered an alternative model of the universe to Ptolemy's geocentric system, which had been widely accepted since ancient times.
commentaries: Umberto Eco mentions Copernicus’s seminal work as the landmark publication that challenged the Ptolemaic system.
Umberto Eco cites Martial's Epigrams as a classical example of hostile female portrayal in literature, using it to illustrate the long-standing tradition of demonizing women in satire.

book:1907.description: Neither Christopher Columbus nor his contemporaries thought the earth was flat. Yet this curious illusion persists today, firmly established with the help of the media, textbooks, teachers--even noted historians. Inventing the Flat Earthis Russell's attempt to set the record straight. He begins with a discussion of geographical knowledge in the Middle Ages, examining what Columbus and his contemporaries actually did believe, and then moves to a look at how the error was first propagated in the 1820s and 183...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Russell's book to debunk the myth that medieval people widely believed in a flat Earth, using it as scholarly evidence against modern misconceptions.

book:831106.description: Edward Gibbon called The Historiesan 'immortal work, every sentence of which is pregnant with the deepest observations and the most lively images.' Its author, Cornelius Tacitus, widely acknowledged as the greatest of all Roman historians, describes with cynical power the murderous 'Year of the Four Emperors' - AD 69 - when in just a few months the whole of the Roman Empire was torn apart by civil war. The ultimate triumph of Vespasian and his sons Titus and Domitian was only the prelude to further conflict...
commentaries: Umberto Eco quotes Tacitus to demonstrate how ancient Roman writers constructed Jewish difference as inherent threat, using ritual practices as symbols of moral alienation.

book:11063671.description: This historic book may have numerous typos and missing text. Purchasers can download a free scanned copy of the original book (without typos) from the publisher. Not indexed. Not illustrated. 1897 Excerpt: ...knowing it had so been written, and seeing in very deed babes and sucklings in an astonishing manner with loud voices chanting the hymn, they reflected that if he could make babes beyond their natural capacity sing the hymn with loud voices, he could also make inanimate things cry out--and thus reflect...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Cosmas's work to illustrate a fringe medieval cosmological model based on biblical imagery, emphasizing its obscurity and lack of influence on medieval thought.

book:13451770.description:
Guy Montag is a fireman. His job is to burn books, which are forbidden, being the source of all discord and unhappiness. Even so, Montag is unhappy; there is discord in his marriage. Are books hidden in his house? The Mechanical Hound of the Fire Department, armed with a lethal hypodermic, escorted by helicopters, is ready to track down those dissidents who defy society to preserve and read books.
The classic novel of a post-literate future, 'Fahrenheit 451' stands alongside Orwell's '1984' and Huxley's 'Br...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Bradbury’s novel as a modern allegory of censorship and the destruction of knowledge through fire.
Umberto Eco cites Bradbury’s novel as a cultural reference point for themes of censorship, fire, and knowledge suppression.

book:web_98ecf81f.description: A pioneering 18th-century essay by French Catholic priest and abolitionist Henri Grégoire advocating for the civil rights and social integration of Jews in France, arguing for their physical, moral, and political regeneration through education and emancipation.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Grégoire’s work as an early example of pseudoscientific reasoning used to attribute negative traits to Jews through dietary habits.

book:web_c78c19f0.description: A theological treatise by Tertullian, an early Christian author, discussing the nature, origin, and immortality of the soul, written in Latin around 207 CE.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Tertullian’s De anima as a key source for the heretical theory of traducianism regarding soul transmission.

book:242897.description: This work contains the 26 visions of Hildegard of Bingen (1098-1179), who was the first of the great German mystics, as well as a poet and a prophet, a physician and a political moralist.
commentaries: Umberto Eco quotes Hildegard’s visionary text to show how medieval Christian mysticism associated the Antichrist with physical deformity and foul odor as signs of divine corruption.
Umberto Eco cites Hildegard of Bingen's Liber scivias as a key example of medieval mystical visions dominated by radiant light and fire.

book:6828985.description: On the eve of his final odes and hymns, Friedrich Holderlin composed three versions of a dramatic poem on the suicide of the early Greek thinker, Empedocles of Acragas. This book offers the first complete translation of the three versions, along with translations of Holderlin's essays on the theory of tragedy. David Farrell Krell gives readers a brief chronology of Holderlin's life, an introduction to the life and thought of Empedocles--including Holderlin's Empedocles--detailed explanatory notes, and an an...
commentaries: Umberto Eco invokes Hölderlin’s play to exemplify the poetic longing for union with fire as a path to divine transcendence.

book:7775986.description: L'inondazione di odio in Internet, i cori negli stadi contro i giocatori neri, il risveglio del demone antisemita, le spedizioni squadristiche contro gli omosessuali, i rimpianti di troppi politici per "i metodi di Hitler", le avanzate in tutta Europa dei partiti xenofobi, le milizie in divisa para-nazista, i pestaggi di disabili, le rivolte veneziane contro gli "zingari" anche se sono veneziani da secoli e fanno di cognome Pavan, gli omicidi di clochard, gli inni immondi alla purezza del sangue... Come a v...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Stella's book as a comprehensive treatment of the same theme, contrasting it with his own shorter essay and acknowledging its scholarly weight.

book:web_87369611.description: A surreal and humorous novel by Italian writer Achille Campanile, first published in 1928, known for its absurd narrative style and satirical tone, characteristic of the Italian avant-garde literature of the interwar period.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Campanile's novel as an example of the literary device of anagnorisis and the false stranger, used with surreal good sense.
Umberto Eco cites Galileo's work as a pivotal but controversial publication in the history of astronomy, noting the resistance it faced.

book:11929497.description: Lucretius' poem On the Nature of Thingscombines a scientific and philosophical treatise with some of the greatest poetry ever written. With intense moral fervour he demonstrates to humanity that in death there is nothing to fear since the soul is mortal, and the world and everything in it is governed by the mechanical laws of nature and not by gods; and that by believing this men can live in peace of mind and happiness. He bases this on the atomic theory expounded by the Greek philosopher Epicurus, and cont...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Lucretius’s De rerum natura as the vehicle through which Epicurus’s materialist cosmology survived into early modern debates.
Umberto Eco quotes Lucretius directly to support the ancient Epicurean argument for an infinite universe and plurality of worlds, treating it as a foundational philosophical concept.

book:46992.description: Bringing together their unique vantage points as leaders of Church and State, Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger and Marcello Pera challenge us to imagine what can be the future of a civilization that has abandoned its moral and cultural history. They call on the West to embrace a spiritual rather than political renewal -and to accept the moral values that alone can help us to make sense of changes in technology, economics, and society.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Pera's book as a key source of secular critique against cultural relativism, highlighting its argument that Western values are superior and that migration patterns indicate cultural preference.
Umberto Eco references Pera’s book as a critique of cultural relativism, highlighting its argument that Western values are superior and universally preferable.

book:web_f479ea80.description: A collection of popular science essays by Italian theoretical physicist Tullio Regge, originally published in 1993, exploring topics in physics, cosmology, and the nature of the universe in an accessible style.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references this work to highlight a scientific critique of science fiction's treatment of instantaneous communication and causality violations.

book:12958554.description:
Utopie, das schone Wort vom Nirgend-Ort, hat am Ende dieses Jahrhunderts seinen Zauberklang verloren. Die Welt ist vermessen, der Bericht von einem unentdeckten Ort, an dem sich besser leben lasst, musste heute aus dem Weltall zu uns dringen, um wenigstens minimale Chancen auf Glaubwurdigkeit zu haben.
In dieser Hinsicht hatte es der Londoner Rechtsgelehrte Thomas More vor fast 500 Jahren einfacher. Amerikas Entdeckung lag 24 Jahre zuruck, da schrieb er einen Bericht uber ein Gesprach mit einem Seefahrer, d...
commentaries: Umberto Eco identifies More’s Utopia as a foundational example of the island utopia genre, emblematic of idealized, unreachable societies.

book:439226.description: The editor of a sci-fi pulp magazine is accidentally transported to a parallel universe where space travel is common, Earth is at war with creepy aliens, New York City isn't safe after dark, and his girlfriend is with someone else. Regularly appears on "Greatest science fiction" lists.
commentaries: Umberto Eco uses this novel to illustrate how science fiction operationalizes the philosophical concept of parallel universes through narrative variation.
Umberto Eco references Brown’s novel as part of a set of foundational science fiction texts relevant to the thesis topic, used to demonstrate how sources are tracked in a work plan.

book:web_bfce77a6.description: A science fiction short story by Fredric Brown, first published in the March 1952 issue of 'Astounding Science Fiction'. It features a lone soldier on a distant planet, reflecting themes of isolation and duty.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Brown’s short story 'Sentry' as a narrative exemplar of the relativity of ugliness and the subjective nature of aesthetic perception.

book:web_a878a56b.description: A novel by Italian writer Luigi Malerba, published in 1990, blending historical fiction with metafictional elements, centered on the mysterious substance known as Greek fire.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Malerba’s novel as a literary treatment of historical military fire, linking it to broader themes of destruction and mystery.

book:19720170.description: Apollonius Rhodius's Argonautica, composed in the 3rd century BCE, is the epic retelling of Jason's quest for the golden fleece. Along with his contemporaries Callimachus and Theocritus, Apollonius refashioned Greek poetry to meet the interests and aesthetics of a Hellenistic audience, especially that of Alexandria in the Ptolemaic period following Alexander's death. In this carefully crafted work of 5,835 hexameter verses in four books, the author draws on the preceding literary traditions of epic (Homer),...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Apollonius of Rhodes’s epic as a classical source of island legends, linking it to the mythic tradition of inaccessible lands.

book:web_11f02a0f.description: A treatise on dairy products by Italian botanist and naturalist Paolo Boccone, published in 1671 as part of his broader scientific writings on plants and natural history.
commentaries: Umberto Eco notes Boccone’s treatise on dairy as one of the obscure historical sources Camporesi uses to build his argument about cheese’s cultural and medical stigma.

book:168501.description: Lucan's epic poem on the civil war between Caesar and Pompey, unfinished at the time of his death, stands beside the poems of Virgil and Ovid in the first rank of Latin epic. This newly annotated, free verse translation conveys the full force of Lucan's writing and his grimly realistic view of the subject. The work is a powerful condemnation of civil war, emphasizing the stark, dark horror of the catastrophies which the Roman state inflicted upon itself. Both the introduction and glossary set the scene for....
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Lucan’s Pharsalia as an example of classical textual transmission and the value placed on literary works in the early Middle Ages.

book:web_20b0e4d1.description: A detailed pilgrimage account written by the Dominican friar Felix Fabri, documenting his travels to the Holy Land, Arabia, and Egypt in the late 15th century. It is one of the most extensive and vivid medieval travel narratives, offering insights into geography, culture, and religious practices of the regions visited.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Felix Fabri's travelogue as a historical source documenting medieval Christian perceptions of Muslim body odor.

book:web_0c6fcf1d.description: A philosophical and theological work by Nicholas of Cusa, written in 1440, which explores the limits of human knowledge and the nature of God through the concept of 'learned ignorance' (docta ignorantia). It is a foundational text of Renaissance humanism and mysticism.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Nicholas of Cusa's De docta ignorantia as a foundational philosophical source for the idea that God, as absolute, is fundamentally unknowable and beyond human conceptualization.

book:132876.description: Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus, 65-8 BCE) was born at Venusia, son of a freedman clerk who had him well educated at Rome and Athens. Horace supported the ill-fated killers of Caesar, lost his property, became a secretary in the Treasury, and began to write poetry. Maecenas, lover of literature, to whom Virgil and Varius introduced Horace in 39, became his friend and made him largely independent by giving him a farm. After 30 Horace knew and aided with his pen the emperor Augustus, who after Virgil's death...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Horace’s Satires to illustrate that witch figures existed in classical literature, but were not yet perceived as societal threats, contrasting them with later medieval and early modern hysteria.
Umberto Eco references Horace's Epistles to show that criticism of new literary works based solely on their recency was already present in antiquity.

book:web_84205a40.description: Edited volume by Francesco Galofaro published by CLUEB in Bologna in 2009, addressing medical research ethics and European cultural identity.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Galofaro as the editor of a volume containing his lecture, indicating the book as the published context of his work.

book:6316119.description: Set in Russia in the midst of its troubled transition to the modern age, this classic novel is the profound human drama of Raskolnikov, a sensitive intellectual driven by poverty and the belief of his exemption from moral law. Through his unforgettable gallery of characters, Dostoyevsky provides a provocative look at the human motivations of obsession and possession with unflinching philosophical and moral insight. A masterpiece of dramatic literature by one of the greatest novelist of all time.
commentaries: Umberto Eco uses Raskolnikov as an example of a character whose destiny is fixed by narrative necessity, directly referencing Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment as the source of the character’s moral and psychological trajectory.

book:web_22cce84e.description: A mytho-hermetic dictionary by Antoine-Joseph Pernety, a French monk and alchemical scholar, compiling symbolic and allegorical terms from alchemical texts. It was published in 1758 as part of his work on esoteric traditions and served as a reference for interpreting alchemical symbolism.
commentaries: Umberto Eco uses Dom Pernety’s Dictionnaire mytho-hermétique to describe the physical and symbolic stages of alchemical transformation, particularly the nigredo phase.
Umberto Eco cites Dom Pernety again to argue that diverse alchemical terminology refers to a single underlying process, emphasizing the unity of alchemical practice.
Umberto Eco references Dom Pernety to show how the alchemical red substance is symbolically equated with fire, blurring the line between material and metaphor.
Umberto Eco references this work as a source on mytho-hermetic thought, likely in the context of esoteric symbolism or alchemical traditions.

book:web_d95fcb2a.description: A medieval manual for inquisitors written by Nicolas Emeric (also known as Nicolau Emeric or Nicholas Eymerich), a Spanish Dominican friar and Inquisitor General of Aragon. It served as a comprehensive guide for identifying, interrogating, and prosecuting heresy in the 14th century and remained influential for centuries.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Emeric’s manual alongside Gui’s as a foundational text in the development of inquisitorial procedures against heresy.

book:2778115.description: That Book ... that perverse Book -- Eleanora DusaFirst published in Italian in 1900, The Flame is one of the most sensational works of the fin-de-siecle and is justifiably notorious due to its being a thinly-veiled account of the author's tempestuous affair with the legendary actress, Eleanora Dusa. A contemporary critic called it the most swinish novel ever written. Sarah Bernhardt returned her presentation copy to the author unopened.Writing in a florid style reminiscent of Henry James and Walter Pater, D...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites D’Annunzio’s novel as the first work to explicitly connect aesthetic ecstasy with the imagery and sensation of fire.
Umberto Eco cites D’Annunzio’s work as an example of aesthetic reverence for fire and its transformative power in literature.
Umberto Eco cites D’Annunzio’s The Flame as a textual parallel to James Joyce’s use of fire imagery in Portrait of the Artist, suggesting a direct literary influence.
Umberto Eco cites D’Annunzio’s The Flame as a source for a translated excerpt included in table 5.1.

book:2767201.description: Auto da fe(1935), primo libro di Elias Canetti e suo unico romanzo, e un'opera solitaria ed estrema, segnata dalla intransigente felicita degli inizi. Qui tutto si svolge nella tensione fra due esseri cresciuti ai capi opposti nelle immense fronde dell'albero della vita: il sinologo Kien e la sua governante Therese. Kien e un grande studioso che disprezza i professori, ritiene superflui e sgradevoli i contatti col mondo, ama in fondo una cosa sola: i libri. E i libri lo circondano e lo proteggono, schierati...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Canetti’s novel to draw a parallel between intellectual self-destruction and the mythic sacrifice by fire.

book:238953.description: Das Kapital, Karl Marx's seminal work, is the book that above all others formed the twentieth century. From Kapitalsprung the economic and political systems that at one time dominated half the earth and for nearly a century kept the world on the brink of war. Even today, more than one billion Chinese citizens live under a regime that proclaims fealty to Marxist ideology. Yet this important tome has been passed over by many readers frustrated by Marx's difficult style and his preoccupation with nineteenth-ce...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Marx's Das Kapital as a literary parallel to Gwynplaine's speech, suggesting its revolutionary content is rendered absurd by his grotesque appearance.
Umberto Eco contrasts Capital with The Communist Manifesto to illustrate how Marx adjusted his style according to audience and purpose.
Umberto Eco cites Marx's work as a foundational text defining ugliness in relation to power and money.
Umberto Eco references Marx's early manuscripts as a foundational text for philosophical or ethical discussions on labor and alienation.

book:969491.description: Regarded as one of the most influential political tracts ever written, The Communist Manifesto serves as the foundation document of the Marxist movement. Originally published on the eve of the 1848 European revolutions, The Communist Manifesto is a condensed and incisive account of the worldview Marx and Engels developed during their hectic intellectual and political collaboration. Formulating the principles of dialectical materialism, they believed that labor creates wealth, hence capitalism is exploitativ...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites The Communist Manifesto as an example of Marx adopting a stylistically unconventional form for rhetorical effect, distinct from his scholarly work.

book:web_ef6606a5.description: A tenth-century eschatological treatise by the Benedictine monk Adso of Montier-en-Der, describing the signs of the end times and the birth, life, and defeat of the Antichrist. It was highly influential in medieval Christian apocalyptic thought.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Adso’s medieval theological letter to illustrate the linkage between Jewish identity and the figure of the Antichrist in Christian eschatology.

book:web_070a8b27.description: A famous world map published in 1570 as part of Abraham Ortelius's atlas 'Theatrum Orbis Terrarum', considered the first modern atlas. The 'Typus orbis terrarum' is the title page map of the atlas, depicting the known world in the late 16th century.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Ortelius’s map as an example of imaginary geography that inadvertently led to real discoveries, framing it as a catalyst for exploration.

Umberto Eco cites Lenin's Materialism and Empirio-criticism to draw a provocative parallel between his materialist epistemology and Aquinas's medieval theory of truth, suggesting an unconscious philosophical continuity.
Umberto Eco cites Lenin’s work to draw a parallel between modern materialist philosophy and medieval Thomism, using it to highlight continuity in theories of truth.

book:771091.description:
For nearly three centuries Malleus Maleficarum (The Witches' Hammer) was the professional manual for witch hunters. This work by two of the most famous Inquisitors of the age is still a document of the forces of that era's beliefs. Under a Bull of Pope Innocent VIII, Kramer and Sprenger exposed the heresy of those who did not believe in witches and set forth the proper order of the world with devils, witches, and the will of God. Even if you do not believe in witchcraft, the world of 1484 did.
Contemporary....
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites the Malleus maleficarum as the seminal and infamous handbook of witch-hunting, directly influenced by earlier texts like Nider’s Formicarius.

book:web_10df02e2.description: A theological and philosophical commentary on the 'Sentences' by Peter Lombard, written by Saint Bonaventure in the mid-13th century. It is a foundational work of medieval scholasticism, particularly influential in Franciscan thought, and covers topics such as the nature of light, being, and divine illumination.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Bonaventure’s Commentary on the Book of Sentences to support the medieval scholastic view that light is the essential, substantial form of all created beings.

book:web_775aa331.description: A theological and philosophical work by Saint Bonaventure, a Franciscan theologian and Doctor of the Church, written as a commentary on Peter Lombard's 'Sentences'. It is a foundational text of medieval scholasticism, integrating Aristotelian philosophy with Augustinian theology.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references this work to illustrate how Bonaventure conceptualized light as the essential substance of all beings, linking metaphysical being with physical radiance.

book:web_2e915c7f.description: A foundational Christian apologetic work by Lactantius, written in the early 4th century, which systematically defends Christianity against pagan beliefs and philosophies.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Lactantius's work as an example of early Christian rejection of the spherical Earth, using biblical literalism to argue for a rectangular cosmos.

book:web_8ada066b.description: An official document published by the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith on June 26, 2000, revealing the third secret of Fatima and providing theological commentary on the apparitions. It is not a book in the traditional sense but an authoritative ecclesiastical publication issued by the Vatican.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this document as a source describing the vision of hell at Fatima, using it to contrast with alchemical fire.

book:6351885.description: The 120 Days of Sodom by Marquis de Sade relates the story of four wealthy men who enslave 24 mostly teenaged victims and sexually torture them while listening to stories told by old prostitutes. The book was written while Sade was imprisoned in the Bastille and the manuscript was lost during the storming of the Bastille. Sade wrote that he "wept tears of blood" over the manuscript's loss. Many consider this to be Sade crowning achievement.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Sade's work as an extreme example of excessive revelation, contrasting it with Dante's restraint to illustrate narrative excess in feuilletons.

book:652336.description:
Weaving early accounts of witchcraft--trial records, ecclesiastical tracts, folklore & popular iconography--into new & startling patterns, Carlo Ginzburg presents in Ecstasiescompelling evidence of a hidden shamanistic culture that flourished across Europe for thousands of years.
Introduction
Lepers, Jews, Muslims
Jews, Heretics, Witches
Following the Goddess
Anomalies
To Combat in Ecstasy
Disguised as Animals
Eurasian Conjectures
Bones & Skin
Conclusion
Index
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Ginzburg’s work as a historical source documenting the persecution of lepers and its connection to later witchcraft narratives.

book:web_9a58c566.description: A philosophical work by Italian moral philosopher Eugenio Lecaldano arguing that a robust ethical framework can be constructed without reference to God, drawing on historical and anthological sources to support secular morality.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Lecaldano’s book as a contemporary argument that morality can be grounded independently of theological belief.
Umberto Eco references this work as a source on secular ethics, indicating its relevance to moral philosophy without divine grounding.

book:web_ecf4000a.description: A 17th-century treatise on subterranean phenomena, minerals, and early geological thought by German physician, alchemist, and philosopher Joachim Becher. It reflects pre-modern theories of earth sciences and was influential in early mineralogy and proto-geology.
commentaries: Umberto Eco presents Becher’s Physica subterranea as one of the forgotten texts Camporesi mines to construct a historical narrative of cheese’s perceived malevolence.

book:436352.description: Ptolemy's Almagest is one of the most influential scientific works in history. A masterpiece of technical exposition, it was the basic textbook of astronomy for more than a thousand years, and still is the main source for our knowledge of ancient astronomy. This translation, based on the standard Greek text of Heiberg, makes the work accessible to English readers in an intelligible and reliable form. It contains numerous corrections derived from medieval Arabic translations and extensive footnotes that take...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Ptolemy’s Almagest as a foundational astronomical text that was studied and translated in the medieval period.

book:2932255.description: Ce livre n'est pas un roman, quoique l'intention en soit romanesque. Il n'appartient pas a la science-fiction, quoiqu'on y cotoie des mythes qui alimentent ce genre. Il n'est pas une collection de faits bizarres, quoique l'Ange du Bizarre s'y trouve a l'aise. Il n'est pas non plus une contribution scientifique, le vehicule d'un enseignement inconnu, un temoignage, un documentaire, ou une affabulation. Il est le recit, parfois legende et parfois exact, d'un premier voyage dans des domaines de la connaissance...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this book as a source attributing Nazi cosmic beliefs to Hitler's propaganda about Arctic superiority.

book:156723.description: In Counter-Clock World, one of the most theologically probing of all of Dick's books, the world has entered the Hobart Phase-a vast sidereal process in which time moves in reverse. As a result, libraries are busy eradicating books, copulation signifies the end of pregnancy, people greet with, "Good-bye," and part with, "Hello," and underneath the world's tombstones, the dead are coming back to life. One imminent old-born is Anarch Peak, a vibrant religious leader whose followers continued to flourish long a...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this novel as an imaginative extension of thermodynamic principles, reversing entropy as a narrative device.

book:123933.description:
Jean-Paul Sartre, the great French existentialist, displays his mastery of drama in NO EXIT, an unforgettable portrayal of hell.
The play is a depiction of the afterlife in which three deceased characters are punished by being locked into a room together for eternity. It is the source of Sartre's especially famous and often misinterpreted quotation "L'enfer, c'est les autres" or "Hell is other people", a reference to Sartre's ideas about the Look and the perpetual ontological struggle of being caused to see...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Sartre's play No Exit as a foundational text illustrating how human relationships become sources of torment when the Other is perceived as intolerable.

book:511340.description: Jean-Paul Sartre, the seminal smarty-pants of mid-century thinking, launched the existentialist fleet with the publication of Being & Nothingnessin 1943. Tho the book is thick, dense & unfriendly to careless readers, it's indispensable to those interested in the philosophy of consciousness & free will. Some of his arguments are fallacious, others are unclear, but for the most part his thoughts penetrate deeply into fundamental philosophical territory. Basing his conception of self-consciousness loosely on H...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Sartre’s Being and Nothingness as the definitive philosophical account of self-deception, using it to introduce the concept of bad faith as a monadic form of lying.

book:web_f12f843c.description: A first-hand account by Liutprand of Cremona, an Italian bishop and diplomat, describing his humiliating embassy to the Byzantine court of Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas in 949. The text is renowned for its vivid, satirical, and hostile portrayal of the Byzantine emperor and court.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Liutprand’s account to illustrate how physical appearance and cultural unfamiliarity were used to dehumanize the Byzantine emperor as an enemy.

book:web_5f81864c.description: A medieval theological and cosmological treatise written in the 12th century by Honorius of Autun, a Benedictine monk and theologian. The work synthesizes biblical, classical, and patristic sources to describe the structure of the world, often incorporating allegorical and symbolic interpretations of geography and nature.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Honorious of Autun's De imagine mundi as a medieval source describing the Lost Island as an elusive paradise, emphasizing its mythical and unattainable nature.

book:web_600de49a.description: A utopian novel by French author Denis Vairasse, published in 1675-1677, describing an imaginary island society called Sévarambes. It was influential in the tradition of utopian literature and often compared to works like Thomas More's Utopia and Foigny's Terra Australis.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Vairasse’s island of Sevarambes as another example of a fictional perfect civilization located on an island.

book:848892.description:
Ever a source of philosophical conjecture and debate, the concept of time represents the beating heart of physics. This final work by the distinguished physicist Hans Reichenbach represents the culmination and integration of a lifetime's philosophical contributions and inquiries into the analysis of time. The result is an outstanding overview of such qualitative, or topological, attributes of time as order and direction.
Beginning with a discussion of the emotive significance of time, Reichenbach turns to a...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references this philosophical work to ground science fiction's treatment of time loops and non-linear causality in formal logical frameworks.

book:web_85c3ce13.description: A 9th-century theological commentary by John Scotus Eriugena on the Pseudo-Dionysian work 'The Celestial Hierarchy,' integrating Neoplatonic philosophy with Christian theology. It is one of the most important works of early medieval philosophy and mysticism.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Eriugena’s Commentary on the Celestial Hierarchy to illustrate the early medieval theological framework that equates God with light and the cosmos with a luminous structure.
Umberto Eco cites this commentary as a foundational medieval text that articulates a cosmology of light, portraying God as the source of all luminous revelation.

book:web_7d894bef.description: A major philosophical work by John Scotus Eriugena, written in the 9th century, which synthesizes Neoplatonism with Christian theology. It is structured in five books and explores the division of nature into categories of being and non-being. The work was later condemned as heretical but remains a cornerstone of medieval philosophy.
commentaries: Umberto Eco invokes Eriugena’s text to support Pareyson’s view that imperfections contribute to the beauty of the whole, drawing on Neoplatonic philosophy to justify the functional necessity of structural flaws.

book:2627504.description:
A best-seller in Spain, Mexico, Venezuela, Argentina, and Brazil: the first-ever world history of the destruction of books.
A product of ten years of research and support from leading American and European universities, "A Universal History of the Destruction of Books" traces a tragic story: the smashed tablets of ancient Sumer, the widespread looting of libraries in post-war Iraq, the leveling of the Library of Alexandria, book burnings by Crusaders and Nazis, and censorship against authors past and presen...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this book as a reference point, likely for its exploration of lost texts or cultural destruction.
Umberto Eco cites Báez’s work to support the thesis that fire’s symbolic role in religion and culture underpins its historical use in book destruction.

book:6086646.description: Written in his distinctively dazzling manner, Oscar Wilde's story of a fashionable young man who sells his soul for eternal youth and beauty is the author's most popular work. The tale of Dorian Gray's moral disintegration caused a scandal when it first appeared in 1890, but though Wilde was attacked for the novel's corrupting influence, he responded that there is, in fact, "a terrible moral in Dorian Gray." Just a few years later, the book and the aesthetic/moral dilemma it presented became issues in the t...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Wilde’s novel through an annotated edition, suggesting it is cited for its exploration of truth, appearance, and moral corruption.

book:24949945.description:
Oscar Wilde's madcap farce about mistaken identities, secret engagements, and lovers' entanglements still delights readers more than a century after its 1895 publication and premiere performance. The rapid-fire wit and eccentric characters of "The Importance of Being Earnest" have made it a mainstay of the high school curriculum for decades.
Cecily Cardew and Gwendolen Fairfax are both in love with the same mythical suitor. Jack Worthing has wooed Gwendolen as Ernest while Algernon has also posed as Ernest....
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Wilde’s play as a published work, likely referencing its themes of deception and social performance.
Umberto Eco references Wilde’s play as a literary example of irony, deception, and performative identity, likely in the context of fictionality and truth.

book:web_b3259e72.description: A collection of epigrams and aphorisms by Oscar Wilde, compiled and published posthumously. Although Wilde died in 1900, this 1907 edition was compiled by others from his published and unpublished writings, reflecting his wit and philosophical observations. The title is likely a later compilation rather than a work originally published by Wilde himself under this exact title.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Wilde’s collection of epigrams as a source of philosophical wit, likely for insights on truth and societal norms.
Umberto Eco lists this essay collection as a published work, indicating it is referenced as a critical source.

book:web_e9c98659.description: A collection of aphorisms and philosophical reflections by the French writer and moralist Sébastien-Roch Nicolas de Chamfort, published posthumously in 1795. The work is renowned for its wit, cynicism, and insight into human nature.
commentaries: Umberto Eco uses Chamfort’s maxim as a clear example of an aphorism that plays with conventional interpretations of wealth and poverty.

book:web_54ab9e33.description: A medieval alchemical text attributed to Artephius, a legendary or possibly pseudonymous figure in Hermetic and alchemical traditions. The work is known for its esoteric teachings on the philosopher's stone and the art of prolonging life, written in symbolic language typical of alchemical literature. It was widely circulated in manuscript form during the Middle Ages and referenced by later alchemists.
commentaries: Umberto Eco quotes Artephius to emphasize the esoteric, deliberately opaque language of alchemical texts, which conceal their true meaning from the uninitiated.

book:606818.description: A nineteenth century French priest discovers something in his mountain village at the foot of The Pyrenees which enables him to amass and spend a fortune of millions of pounds. The tale seems to begin with buried treasure and then turns into an unprecedented historical detective story - a modern Grail quest leading back through cryptically coded parchments, secret societies, the Knights Templar, the Cathar heretics of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries and a dynasty of obscure French kings deposed more th...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Lincoln’s book, co-authored with Leigh and Baigent, as the vehicle that amplified the Rennes-le-Château myth to a wide public after its media exposure.
Umberto Eco cites this modern work as a source on esoteric conspiracy theories surrounding the Holy Grail, likely to analyze myth-making or fictional historiography.

book:web_2455e5b6.description: A critical essay by Italian philosopher Benedetto Croce on the nature of poetry, published in 1936 as part of his broader aesthetic and philosophical writings. It explores the emotional and moral dimensions of poetic creation.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Croce's book as a foundational text distinguishing poetic moments from structural elements in literature, using it to frame the debate on imperfections and padding in poetry.

book:web_c290073d.description: A foundational history of aesthetics by the Italian philosopher Benedetto Croce, originally published in 1928, tracing the development of aesthetic thought from antiquity to the modern era.
commentaries: Umberto Eco includes Croce’s 1928 work as one of the classic histories of aesthetics encountered in the Treccani’s references, implying its relevance to the historical development of aesthetic theory.

book:9456.description:
This is a new translation, with running commentary, of what is perhaps the most important short piece of Hegel's writing. The Preface to Hegel's first major work, the Phenomenology of Spirit, lays the groundwork for all his other writing by explaining what is most innovative about Hegel's philosophy.
This new translation combines readability with maximum precision, breaking Hegel's long sentences and simplifying their often complex structure. At the same time, it is more faithful to the original than any pr...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Hegel’s philosophical work as a key text, referencing the original author despite the translation.

book:23883012.description: Hegel's "Logic" is one of the culminating breakthroughs of modern philosophy, containing the most thorough explanation of "dialectic" that Hegel ever wrote, and setting the stage for his "Philosophy of Nature" and "Philosophy of Mind." This translation by William Wallace, White's Professor of Moral Philosophy at Oxford University, has been long recognized as a benchmark text for English translations of Hegel and of German philosophy in general. Prof. Wallace's introductory essay, explaining the origin of He...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Hegel’s work as an example of a dense, complex text that cannot be easily annotated in the original and requires alternative methods like photocopies and notebooks.

book:127236.description: A collection of studies in which Arendt, from the standpoint of a political philosopher, views the crises of the 1960s and early 1970s as challenges to the american form of government.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Arendt's work as a key philosophical analysis of political deception, highlighting her argument that lies have historically been accepted as tools in politics, though she later condemns systemic lying as an offense against factuality.

book:web_bab325bd.description: A philosophical work by German philosopher Karl Rosenkranz that systematically explores the concept of ugliness as a counterpart to beauty in aesthetics, published in 1853. It is considered one of the first major treatises devoted exclusively to ugliness in art and philosophy.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Rosenkrantz's book as a rare and significant historical text dedicated explicitly to the aesthetics of ugliness.

book:484422.description: Wuthering Heightsis a wild, passionate story of the intense and almost demonic love between Catherine Earnshaw and Heathcliff, a foundling adopted by Catherine's father. After Mr. Earnshaw's death, Heathcliff is bullied and humiliated by Catherine's brother Hindley and wrongly believing that his love for Catherine is not reciprocated, leaves Wuthering Heights, only to return years later as a wealthy and polished man. He proceeds to exact a terrible revenge for his former miseries. The action of the story is...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Heathcliff and Catherine from Wuthering Heights to illustrate the inescapable fate of fictional characters, grounding the example in Emily Brontë’s novel as the definitive textual source.

book:web_246aaaac.description: A foundational work in medieval logic by William of Ockham, systematically presenting his theory of signification, supposition, and propositional logic. It is one of the most influential logical treatises of the 14th century and a key text in the development of nominalism.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Ockham’s argument from Summa logicae to explore the limits of iconic representation, using it to question how the sacred—an entity beyond experience—can be visually rendered.

Umberto Eco references Ockham’s semiotic theory in Summa logicae to distinguish between concepts as primary signs and words as secondary signs, reinforcing the epistemological argument about the foundations of meaning.
Umberto Eco cites this logical treatise as a cornerstone of Ockham's nominalist philosophy.

book:web_52c569b5.description: A commentary on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, written by the English Franciscan friar and philosopher William of Ockham. It is one of his major theological works and contains early formulations of his famous principle of parsimony, later known as Occam's Razor.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites William of Ockham's commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences as a foundational theological text.
Umberto Eco cites Merton's book as a reference point, likely for its thematic exploration of intellectual lineage and scholarly tradition.

book:web_3f0f0064.description: An ancient Sanskrit scripture of Hinduism, part of the Indian epic Mahabharata, presenting a dialogue between Prince Arjuna and the god Krishna on duty, morality, and the nature of the self.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites the Bhagavad-Gita as a sacred text whose imagery of divine fire resonates with the atomic bomb’s detonation and its existential weight.

book:194457.description: The first English translation of the major political works of Benjamin Constant (1767-1830), one of the most important of the French political figures in the aftermath of the revolution of 1789, and a leading member of the liberal opposition to Napoleon and later to the restored Bourbon monarchy. The texts included in this volume are widely regarded as one of the classic formulations of modern liberal doctrine.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Constant to present a consequentialist counterpoint to Kant, arguing that truth-telling is not absolute when it causes harm.
Umberto Eco cites Constant’s political writings, likely for insights into political deception or the role of truth in governance.

book:web_e4ecc90c.description: A groundbreaking philosophical work by Baruch Spinoza that argues for freedom of thought and expression, and critiques the political use of religion. It was published anonymously in 1670 and is considered a foundational text of biblical criticism and secular political theory.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Spinoza's work to illustrate historical awareness of state secrecy and public exclusion from political knowledge.

book:93839.description: 'This year I intend to begin writing freely about a topic which, in the past, I have hesitated to mention even here. commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Tanizaki’s novel The Key to exemplify cultural relativity in perceptions of bodily perfection, contrasting Japanese and Western ideals of feminine form.

book:web_8b258cb2.description: A collection of poems by Italian poet Olindo Guerrini, published under the pseudonym Lorenzo Stecchetti. 'La canzone dell'odio' ('The Song of Hate') is one of his most famous and controversial works, known for its graphic, vengeful imagery directed at political enemies, particularly those associated with the Papal States. It was first published in 1877 as part of his volume 'Postuma'.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Guerrini's poem as an example of Italian literary engagement with grotesque imagery and moral torment, paralleling Baudelaire's themes.

book:3079681.description: Shipwrecked and cast adrift. Lemuel Gulliver wakes to find himself on Lilliput. an island inhabited by little people. whose height makes their quarrels over fashion and fame seem ridiculous. commentaries: Umberto Eco references Swift’s satire as a literary device to explore the boundaries between fiction and deception, particularly in the context of falsehood and societal critique.

book:2175436.description: This joyous play, the last comedy of Shakespeare's career, sums up his stagecraft with a display of seemingly effortless skill. Prospero, exiled Duke of Milan, living on an enchanted island, has the opportunity to punish and forgive his enemies when he raises a tempest that drives them ashore--as well as to forestall a rebellion, to arrange the meeting of his daughter, Miranda, with an eminently suitable young prince, and, more important, to relinquish his magic powers in recognition of his advancing age. commentaries: Umberto Eco lists this play as a published work, indicating it is referenced as a literary source.

book:2834606.description: One of the greatest plays of all time, the compelling tragedy of the tormented young prince of Denmark continues to capture the imaginations of modern audiences worldwide. The ghost, Hamlet's feigned madness, Ophelia's death and burial, the play within a play, the "closet scene" in which Hamlet accuses his mother of complici...
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Hamlet as an example of a fictional character bound to an ineluctable destiny, invoking Shakespeare’s tragedy as the canonical source of the character’s narrative structure.

book:224740.description: Nobody ever walked across the bridge at night. But on the foggy night that Hammer took that chance, his encounter with a gun-toting thug and a girl on the lam ended with both strangers dead. Soon Hammer is caught in a web of sinister gangsters and beautiful women the likes of which he's never seen -- and his only way out is to kill and kill again...even with his bare hands.
commentaries: Umberto Eco lists this novel as a published work, indicating it is referenced as a literary source.

book:10452057.description: This classic remains one of Karl Popper's most wide-ranging and popular works, notable not only for its acute insight into the way scientific knowledge grows, but also for applying those insights to politics and to history.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references this later work by Popper to reinforce the argument that the conspiracy theory of society is a modern echo of ancient theistic explanations, specifically comparing it to Homeric divine conspiracies.

book:2419446.description:
These Letters, written in defense of his Jansenist friends, exposes and ridicules the doctrines of the Jesuits. Pascal does a wonderful job of being humorous while still making a valid point.
Please Note: This book is easy to read in true text, not scanned images that can sometimes be difficult to decipher.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Pascal's work as an example of rhetorical and theological polemic, situating it within discussions of deception and institutional critique.

book:web_6c366f3d.description: Themis aurea (1618) is a seminal alchemical and philosophical work by Michael Maier, a German physician, alchemist, and courtier. It presents a symbolic and allegorical exploration of alchemical principles, including the idea of a secret brotherhood of adepts, and is considered one of the most important texts of early 17th-century Hermeticism.
