Umberto Eco references Iamblichus's biographical account of Pythagoras as a foundational text on ancient philosophical mysticism.

book:314762.description: Questa edizione dell'opera di Torquato Accetto non solo ci restituisce un testo estremamente singolare, non solo ci rivela nell'umbratile secentesco un grande, temerario retore; ma ci propone un esempio che riconduce ad un'idea della letteratura, idea che non e meramente barocca; la letteratura e una misteriosa, emblematica epifania di parole, che agiscono anche dove tacciono: essa non teme le altezze della teologia positiva, e gli <>della teologia negativa; non ha luogo, ma penetra dovunque, anche nella pr...
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Accetto’s Dissimulazione onesta as a nuanced defense of dissimulation as a practical virtue in a deceptive world, contrasting it with Kant’s moral rigidity.

Umberto Eco cites this treatise as a key text on the ethics and aesthetics of dissimulation, particularly in relation to deception and social conduct.

Mais le vertige et la demesure furent plus forts que les reactionnaires : Maldoror, le double malefique de Lautreamont, en crachant son poi...
commentaries: Umberto Eco presents Lautréamont's work as a radical precursor to avant-garde aesthetics, using extreme bodily horror to reject classicism and conventional beauty.

book:web_f0dbf2de.description: A French book by Gérard de Sède that popularized the myth of the Priory of Sion and the alleged treasure of Rennes-le-Château, including the reproduction of forged parchments attributed to Pierre Plantard. It played a key role in the emergence of modern conspiracy theories surrounding the Holy Grail and secret societies.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites de Sède's book as the pivotal work that popularized the Priory of Sion conspiracy, linking it to the Saunière legend and the fabricated parchments.

book:2234581.description:
'Por sorprendente que resulte al sentido comun, el cerebro de los vertebrados debe su continuo crecimiento y capacidad de adaptacion a su imperfeccion, mientras que el de los invertebrados, mucho mas perfecto desde el punto de vista morfologico, casi no evoluciona. Esta tesis constituye el punto de partida de Elogio de la imperfeccion,....

Umberto Eco cites this work as a contemporary philosophical or scientific reflection on the value of imperfection, used to support aesthetic or ethical arguments.

Written in the early 13th century, it reflects his efforts to reconcile faith and reason.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites William of Auvergne’s treatise to demonstrate how medieval theology equated physical deviation from normative standards with moral or aesthetic imperfection.

book:web_a943b4b9.description: An early Christian apocryphal text, likely composed in the 4th–5th century, written in Syriac, containing liturgical and disciplinary instructions attributed to the risen Christ. Translated into English by James Cooper and Arthur John Maclean in the late 19th century.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this ancient text as a translated religious work, referencing its original authorship despite the translation.

book:677923.description: One of the major political figures of his time, Sir Francis Bacon (1561-1626) served in the court of Elizabeth I and ultimately became Lord Chancellor under James I in 1617. Umberto Eco cites Bacon’s essay as a key historical analysis of deception and strategic concealment in human behavior.

book:web_72e07145.description: An essay by Friedrich Schiller exploring the psychological and aesthetic appeal of tragedy in art, part of his broader philosophical writings on aesthetics and human nature.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Schiller’s essay to support the argument that humans are psychologically drawn to horrifying imagery despite repulsion.

book:522465.description: The remarkable best-seller -- a long-lost, 300-year-old book of wisdom on how to live successfully yet responsibly in a society governed by self-interest -- as acute as Machiavelli yet as humanistic and scrupulously moral as Marcus Aurelius.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Gracián’s The Art of Worldly Wisdom as a central baroque text advocating strategic deception and prudence in social life, contrasting its pragmatic ethos with Accetto’s more restrained view.

An ardent devourer of sentimental novels, she longs for passion and seeks escape in fantasies of high romance, in voracious spending and, eventually, in adultery. But even her affairs bring her disappointment, and when real life continues to fail to live up to her romantic expectations, the consequences are devastating. Flaubert's erotically charged and psychologically acute portrayal of...
commentaries: Umberto Eco uses Madame Bovary as a central example of a fluctuating semiotic object, directly referencing Stendhal’s novel as the source of the character’s defining properties.

book:web_d43553ec.description: A poem by Italian poet Giosuè Carducci, part of his collection 'Rime Nuove' (1865), which celebrates rebellion and secular humanism, famously invoking Satan as a symbol of intellectual and political freedom against religious dogma.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Carducci’s poem as an example of rebellious or transgressive literary expression, likely in relation to themes of defiance or moral inversion.

book:web_7a4d50da.description: A spiritual diary written by Maria Maddalena de' Pazzi, a Carmelite mystic and saint, detailing her visions and religious experiences over forty days in 1598. The text was originally composed in Italian and later published in various editions, including the 1996 Sellerio edition cited.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references this mystical diary as a primary account of divine revelation.

book:web_c4ca58bb.description: A fictionalized biography of Aesop, written in the Hellenistic period, blending legend and folklore about the legendary fabulist. It survives in later Byzantine recensions and is not attributable to a single known author.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this Hellenic text to illustrate how physical ugliness was attributed to Aesop, contrasting his moral and intellectual value with his appearance.

book:web_8f0befc3.description: A popular logic puzzle book by Raymond Smullyan that uses combinatory logic and bird-themed metaphors to explore concepts in mathematical logic, including fixed-point combinators and the lambda calculus.
commentaries: Umberto Eco lists this book as a published work, implying it is referenced as a source of logical puzzles or philosophical ideas.

book:web_a203a970.description: Autobiographical work by Saint Teresa of Ávila, a Spanish Carmelite nun and mystic, detailing her spiritual journey and experiences of divine grace. Originally written in Spanish around 1562, it is a foundational text of Christian mysticism.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Teresa's autobiography as a seminal work on personal spiritual experience and reform.

book:web_f47ae9fa.description: A chapter in the edited volume 'Semantics: An Interdisciplinary Reader in Philosophy, Linguistics and Psychology,' where Noam Chomsky presents key ideas from his generative grammar framework, exploring the relationship between syntactic structures and semantic interpretation.

book:web_e0b7cbda.description: An influential article by Noam Chomsky published in 1966 in the journal 'Revue Roumaine de Linguistique', discussing fundamental constants in linguistic theory, particularly in relation to generative grammar and the autonomy of syntax.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references Chomsky's 1965b publication to trace the evolution of his theoretical stance on semantic interpretation.

book:web_d2dec941.description: An article by Noam Chomsky published in Diogenes (Fall 1965), discussing enduring themes in linguistic theory, reflecting his generative grammar framework and critiques of structuralist approaches.
commentaries: Umberto Eco references this article to illustrate the early development of Chomsky's evolving stance on syntax and semantics.

commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Diderot’s Encyclopédie as a seminal Enlightenment work, likely invoked in discussions of knowledge, rationalism, or progress.

book:web_a37e6fb5.description: A 17th-century Italian work by Giuseppe Battista that presents emblematic representations of fraud and simulation, offering a rhetorical and moral defense of deception as a tool in political and social life.

book:web_a57fb328.description: A comprehensive biography of the French philosopher René Descartes, written by Adrien Baillet and first published in 1691. It is one of the earliest and most detailed biographies of Descartes, drawing on personal letters, eyewitness accounts, and contemporary sources.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Baillet’s biography to illustrate how Descartes used public visibility to refute rumors of secret membership, reinforcing the link between secrecy and invisibility.
Umberto Eco references this biography as a source on Descartes’ life, likely for historical or intellectual context.

book:web_8d54ff79.description: A mystical spiritual work by Saint Maddalena de' Pazzi, an Italian Carmelite nun and mystic, composed of her visions and ecstatic utterances. commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this work as a key example of female mystical expression, highlighting its erotic and ecstatic language directed toward divine love.

book:web_f826ffa5.description: Harald Weinrich was a German literary scholar and linguist known for his work on rhetoric, semiotics, and the philosophy of language. commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Weinrich’s book as a source for identifying linguistic and performative signals of irony, treating it as an authoritative reference on the mechanics of deceptive speech.

book:web_5dce4c70.description: A scholarly work by British anthropologist Raymond Firth exploring the role of symbols in human society, particularly in the context of religion, ritual, and social organization. The book includes analyses of religious symbolism, including references to Catholic mysticism such as Saint Marguerite Marie Alacoque.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites this book as a source for understanding the cultural context of mystical visions, specifically linking it to shifting scientific and popular beliefs about the heart.
Umberto Eco references Firth's anthropological study as a source on symbolic systems in culture.

book:web_564ffff8.description: A mathematical and artistic treatise by Luca Pacioli on the golden ratio, illustrated by Leonardo da Vinci, exploring proportions in geometry, architecture, and art.

book:web_12588702.description: A 2013 academic article published in the Journal of Applied Social Psychology, examining how exposure to conspiracy theories reduces political engagement.
commentaries: Umberto Eco cites Jolley and Douglas's study to support the claim that conspiracy theories discourage political engagement.

q: It must be clear that my subject matter is what Jakobson called translation proper (that is, from one natural language into another).

Here I feel embarrassed, because I have to criticise one of the scholars I have most admired in my life, and whom I still consider a master and an unforgettable friend – the late Roman Jakobson. But Jakobson was once responsible for a possible confusion. Translation and interpretation In his essay on the linguistic aspects of translation, Jakobson (1959) suggested that there are three types of translation: intralinguistic, interlinguistic and intersemiotic.

that I have decided to consider as cases of interpretation but not as cases of translation. There are cases in which, in order to make the meaning of a word or of a sentence clear, we use an interpretant (in the Peircean sense) expressed in a different semiotic system. Think for instance what happens when I explain the sense of a verbal utterance by ostension, that is, when we use an object to ‘translate’ the meaning of a verbal expression, or the inverse, as when a child points his or her finger towards a car and I say that it is a car. In all the above cases, certainly, the new expression aims at interpreting a previous expression, but in different circumstances the same device could interpret different expressions. If we use the term to translate in a metaphorical sense, many interpretations are forms of translation (and in the case of a silent language that reproduces the letters of the alphabet by given gestures it will be a form of transliteration). In passing from certain semiotic systems to others these forms of interpretation act as though they were interpretations by synonymy – with the same limits and strictures that hold for verbal synonymy. But other cases would hardly be defined as translations, not even in a metaphorical sense. If one wants to explain the verbal expression Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony in C Minor, one can undergo the effort of showing the ‘real’ musical object (by playing a disc or by taking the interlocutor to a concert hall). But usually one can sol-fa the beginning of that symphony (hoping that the musical memory of the interlocutor will do the rest). Likewise if somebody asks me what composition has just been broadcast on the radio, I can say it is Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony in C Minor. A sufficient interpretation could also be to answer that this is one of Beethoven’s symphonies. Anyway, what characterises all those interpretations is the fact that the interpretant belongs to a different semiotic system from the interpretandum, and that their difference is due to the fact that their substance is produced by the segmentation of a different continuum or matter. If I recite Hamlet in Italian I change the form and the substance of the expression, but I remain within the boundaries of the same continuum or matter (sounds produced by a human throat). If on the contrary I represent Hamlet killing Polonius in a painting I have changed the expression matter. Differences in continuum or matter are fundamental in a semiotic theory. Think for instance of the various debates on the presumed omnipotence or effability of verbal language. Lotman said that verbal language is the primary modelling system but it cannot translate everything into its own terms. Hjelmslev7 distinguished between limited and unlimited languages. For instance, the language of formal logic is limited in comparison to a natural language: given the most elementary logical formula (p ⊃ q) one can not only translate into English (if P then Q) but also variously interpret (if smoke then fire, if fever then illness), or even, counterfactually, If Napoleon were a woman then he would have married Talleyrand. On the contrary, given the sentence If your son John has your own family name then it means that you have legally acknowledged him, it is true that in a logical language it can be translated as p ⊃ q, but nobody could trace the original sentence from the formula. It seems difficult to translate into words what is expressed by Beethoven’s Fifth, as it is also impossible to ‘translate’ into music the whole Critique of Pure Reason. The phenomenon of ekphrasis permits one to describe an image by words, but no ekphrasis of The Marriage of the Virgin by Raphael can render either the perspective we see when looking at the painting, or the soft harmony of the colours. Let us now consider the importance that a change in matter takes in cases of so-called intersemiotic translation, that one that Jakobson defined as transmutation and that is sometimes called adaptation.
